ℓ\ell-Interval Parking Functions:
Foata invariance, statistic generating functions, and ciphers

Kyle Celano K. CelanoDepartment of Mathematics, Wake Forest University, NC 27109 Email address: celanok@wfu.edu , Jennifer Elder J. ElderDepartment of Computer Science, Mathematics and Physics, Missouri Western State University, St. Joseph, MO 64507 Email address: jelder8@missouriwestern.edu , Kimberly P. Hadaway K. P. HadawayDepartment of Mathematics, Iowa State University, Ames, IA 50010 Email address: kph3@iastate.edu , Pamela E. Harris P. E. HarrisDepartment of Mathematical Sciences, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI 53211 Email address: peharris@uwm.edu , Jeremy L. Martin J. L. MartinDepartment of Mathematics, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS 66045 Email address: jlmartin@ku.edu , Amanda Priestley A. PriestleyDepartment of Mathematics, King’s College London, London, WC2R 2LS United Kingdom Email address: amanda.priestley@kcl.ac.uk and Gabe Udell G. UdellMathematics Department, University of California, Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA 95064 Email address: gudell@ucsc.edu
Date: September 19, 2026
Abstract.

We study enumerative properties of the set IPFℓ⁡(n)\IPF_{\ell}(n): parking functions of length nn in which each car parks at most ℓ\ell spaces past its preferred spot. First, we prove that IPF1⁡(n)\IPF_{1}(n) and IPF2⁡(n)\IPF_{2}(n) are each invariant under the well-known Foata bijection that interchanges inversions and major index, implying that these statistics are equidistributed on IPFℓ⁡(n)\IPF_{\ell}(n). Second, we obtain explicit generating functions for IPF1⁡(n)\IPF_{1}(n) and IPF2⁡(n)\IPF_{2}(n) by inversions and displacement, as well as a cyclic sieving phenomenon for IPF1⁡(n)\IPF_{1}(n). Third, we obtain formulas for the number of elements of IPFℓ⁡(n)\IPF_{\ell}(n) with given sum, using a generalization of Lehmer codes and a bijection due to Avalos and Bly.

Key words and phrases: 
Parking function, ℓ\ell-interval parking function, unit interval parking function, unit Fubini ranking, Lehmer code, ordered set partition, permutation, Foata bijection, cyclic sieving, qq-analogue, inversion, major index, displacement
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 05A05; Secondary 05A15, 05A19

1. Introduction

This paper is about enumerating ℓ\ell-interval parking functions with respect to statistics such as inversion, displacement, and major index. Parking functions first appeared in the work of Konheim and Weiss [19] and have become standard objects in combinatorics. Suppose that nn cars attempt to park in nn spots 1,2,…,n1,2,\dots,n on a one-way street. Each car drives to its preferred spot aia_{i} and parks there if possible; if that spot is taken, the car continues along the street and parks in the first available spot. If all cars are able to park successfully, the tuple α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈[n]n\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in[n]^{n} is called a parking function. In this case, if the iith car parks in spot sis_{i}, then the number si−ais_{i}-a_{i} is its displacement.

An ℓ\ell-interval parking function, or IPF for short, is a parking function in which each car has displacement less than or equal to some fixed number ℓ\ell; we write IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell) for the set of all ℓ\ell-interval parking functions of length nn. These objects were first studied by Aguilar-Fraga et al. [2]. (The idea of restricting each car to an interval was considered by Colaric et al. [8], although in that paper the intervals were not required to have the same length.) The case ℓ=1\ell=1 is of particular interest. These unit interval parking functions, or UPFs, are enumerated by the Fubini numbers [5, 17], which also count the faces of the permutahedron [7]. UPFs are also related to Boolean intervals in weak Bruhat order on the symmetric group [10]. Enumerative results on ℓ\ell-interval parking functions with ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 also give connections to Dyck paths with restricted heights and to preferential arrangements [2].

Bradt et al. [5, Theorem 2.9] proved that unit interval parking functions exhibit a tightly controlled block structure, which we describe in Section 2.2. To summarize, if α=(a1,…,an)\alpha=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}) is a UPF with weakly increasing rearrangement α↑=(a1′,…,an′)\alpha^{\uparrow}=(a^{\prime}_{1},\dots,a^{\prime}_{n}), then ai′∈{i,i−1}a^{\prime}_{i}\in\{i,i-1\} for every ii, and if α↑\alpha^{\uparrow} is partitioned into blocks by inserting a separator before every entry with αi′=i\alpha^{\prime}_{i}=i, then the elements of each block appear left-to-right in α\alpha. This structure is key to many of the enumerative results in this paper. No analogous structure is known for ℓ\ell-interval parking functions with ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2.

In Section 3, we prove that the inversion and major index statistics are equidistributed on ℓ\ell-interval parking functions when ℓ≤2\ell\leq 2 or ℓ≥n−2\ell\geq n-2. Recall that the major index of (w1,w2,…,wn)∈ℤn(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} is maj⁡(w)=∑i∈Des⁡(w)i\maj(w)=\sum_{i\in\Des(w)}i, where Des⁡(w)={i∈[n−1]:wi>wi+1}\Des(w)=\{i\in[n-1]\colon w_{i}>w_{i+1}\}. Foata [13] famously constructed a content-preserving bijection FF on the set of words over a fixed alphabet with the property that inv⁡(F⁡(w))=maj⁡(w)\inv(F(w))=\maj(w), thus proving that the two statistics are equidistributed on any set of words invariant under permutation (as proved earlier by MacMahon [20]). Parking functions are invariant under permutation, but in general, the set of ℓ\ell-interval parking functions is not. Nevertheless, we prove (Theorem 3.1) that Foata’s bijection preserves the set IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell) precisely when ℓ∈{0,1,2,n−2,n−1}\ell\in\{0,1,2,n-2,n-1\}. The most difficult cases are ℓ=1\ell=1 and ℓ=2\ell=2. Along the way, we prove several results (Lemma 3.4, Proposition 3.5, Lemma 3.6) to describe how small changes in a parking function (such as transposing two consecutive entries) affect where the cars park; these facts may be of independent interest and utility.

In Section 4, we study the generating function Φn,ℓ​(q,t)\Phi_{n,\ell}(q,t) for IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell) by total displacement and inversion number. In [6], a subset of the authors found tt-exponential generating functions for Φn,n−1​(1,t)\Phi_{n,n-1}(1,t) and Φn,1​(1,t)\Phi_{n,1}(1,t). In this, we provide succinct formulas Φn,ℓ​(q,t)\Phi_{n,\ell}(q,t) for ℓ∈{1,2,n−2}\ell\in\{1,2,n-2\} (Theorem 4.4, Theorem 4.12, Corollary 4.2). By the Foata invariance of Section 3, this also give us formulas for the displacement-major index generating functions Corollary 4.1. For unit interval parking functions, if we write Φn,1​(q,t)=∑kqk​fn,k​(t)\Phi_{n,1}(q,t)=\sum_{k}q^{k}f_{n,k}(t), then each polynomial fn,k​(t)f_{n,k}(t) exhibits a cyclic sieving phenomenon (Theorem 4.7). Additionally, we derive a general formula in Theorem 4.3 for generating functions of the form ∑α∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)qdisp⁡(α)​tstat⁡(carα)\sum_{\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\operatorname{stat}(\car_{\alpha})} where carα\car_{\alpha} is the permutation carα⁡(i)\car_{\alpha}(i) denotes the car that parks in spot ii and stat:𝔖n→ℂ\operatorname{stat}:\mathfrak{S}_{n}\to\mathbb{C}. When ℓ=1\ell=1 and stat\operatorname{stat} is the number of inversions, this is the same as Φn,1\Phi_{n,1} and reduces to the relatively simple expression in Theorem 4.4. The case ℓ=n−1\ell=n-1 was previously obtained in [9].

In Section 5, we present a method for calculating upfn,kinv\upf_{n,k}^{\inv}, the number of UPFs of length nn with exactly kk inversions. The main tool is a collection of new combinatorial objects called “ciphers”. These are in bijection with UPFs and appeared implicitly in work of Avalos and Bly [4]. We work out explicit formulas for k≤3k\leq 3 (Equations (33)–(35)). The formulas suggest that upfn,kinv=O⁡(2n−2​k​nk)\upf_{n,k}^{\inv}=O(2^{n-2k}n^{k}) in general (Conjecture 5.5). As another application of ciphers, we recover the main result of [10], a bijection between unit Fubini rankings (UPFs with all blocks of sizes 1 or 2) and Boolean intervals in weak order (Theorem 5.8).

We conclude in Section 6 with some open problems for future study.

2. Background

In this section, we provide background and definitions related to parking functions and ℓ\ell-interval parking functions. A standard source for the basics of parking functions is [26]. For interval and ℓ\ell-interval parking functions, see, e.g., [2, 5, 8].

Remark 2.1.

Throughout we interchangeably regard tuples (a1,a2,…,an)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) and words a1a2⋯ana_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n} as identical objects, depending on context.

Throughout, the symbol ℕ\mathbb{N} denotes the set of positive integers. For m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbb{N}, we set [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\} and [m,n]={m,m+1,…,n}[m,n]=\{m,m+1,\dots,n\}. For a tuple α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, we write α↑\alpha^{\uparrow} for the tuple obtained by sorting the elements of α\alpha in weakly increasing order. The symbol 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} denotes the symmetric group of permutations of [n][n]. Throughout, we write permutations in one-line notation.

2.1. Parking functions and ℓ\ell-interval parking functions

We write PFn\PF_{n} for the set of parking functions of length nn. The number of parking functions of length nn is |PFn|=(n+1)n−1|\PF_{n}|=(n+1)^{n-1} [19]. Moreover, a tuple α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈[n]n\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in[n]^{n} is a parking function if and only if its weakly increasing rearrangement α↑=(a1′,a2′,…,an′)\alpha^{\uparrow}=(a^{\prime}_{1},a^{\prime}_{2},\dots,a^{\prime}_{n}) satisfies ai′≤ia^{\prime}_{i}\leq i for all ii, or equivalently if there is some permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that ai≤σia_{i}\leq\sigma_{i} for all i∈[n]i\in[n] [26, p. 4]. It follows that if α∈PFn\alpha\in\PF_{n} and β=(b1,b2,…,bn)\beta=(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n}) satisfy 1≤bi≤ai1\leq b_{i}\leq a_{i} for all i∈[n]i\in[n], then β∈PFn\beta\in\PF_{n}. We refer to this property as the rearrangement criterion.

We write PFn↑\PF_{n}^{\uparrow} for the set of weakly increasing parking functions of length nn. The number of weakly increasing parking functions of length is |PFn↑|=Catn=1n+1​(2​nn)|\PF_{n}^{\uparrow}|=\mathrm{Cat}_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}, the nnth Catalan number [24, Exercise 6.19(s)].

Definition 2.2.

Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈PFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\PF_{n}. The car permutation of α\alpha is carα=(carα⁡(1),…,carα⁡(n))∈𝔖n\car_{\alpha}=(\car_{\alpha}(1),\dots,\car_{\alpha}(n))\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, where carα⁡(i)\car_{\alpha}(i) denotes the car that parks in the iith spot. The spot permutation of α\alpha is spotα=(spotα⁡(1),…,spotα⁡(n))∈𝔖n\spot_{\alpha}=(\spot_{\alpha}(1),\dots,\spot_{\alpha}(n))\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, where spotα⁡(i)\spot_{\alpha}(i) denotes the number of spot that the iith car parks in. Note carα\car_{\alpha} and spotα\spot_{\alpha} are permutations written as tuples and carα=spotα−1\car_{\alpha}=\spot_{\alpha}^{-1}.

Example 2.3.

If α=(1,4,4,3,2,2)∈PFn\alpha=(1,4,4,3,2,2)\in\PF_{n}, then carα=(1,5,4,2,3,6)\car_{\alpha}=(1,5,4,2,3,6) and spotα=(1,4,5,3,2,6)\spot_{\alpha}=(1,4,5,3,2,6).

Remark 2.4.

Much of the parking function literature uses the term “outcome” for what we have called the car permutation of a parking function α\alpha. We have adopted the terms “car permutation” and “spot permutation” because we work with both of them in different parts of this paper, and wish to avoid any possible ambiguity in the use of the word “outcome”. In the Sage ParkingFunctions library, the car permutation is computed as alpha.cars_permutation() and the spot permutation is alpha.parking_permutation().

Definition 2.5.

Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈PFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\PF_{n}. The displacement of the iith car is dispα⁡(i)=spotα⁡(i)−ai\disp_{\alpha}(i)=\spot_{\alpha}(i)-a_{i}. That is, dispα⁡(i)\disp_{\alpha}(i) is the number of additional spaces car ii has to drive past its preferred spot in order to park. The (total) displacement11 1 Total displacement is also called area, since it is exactly the area under the labeled Dyck path representing α\alpha; see, e.g., [26, pp. 54–55]. of α\alpha is disp⁡(α)=∑i=1ndispα⁡(i)\disp(\alpha)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\disp_{\alpha}(i). The maximum displacement of α\alpha is maxdisp⁡(α)=max⁡(dispα⁡(1),dispα⁡(2),…,dispα⁡(n))\maxdisp(\alpha)=\max(\disp_{\alpha}(1),\disp_{\alpha}(2),\dots,\disp_{\alpha}(n)).

Example 2.6 (Continuing Example 2.3).

If α=(1,4,4,3,2,2)∈PFn\alpha=(1,4,4,3,2,2)\in\PF_{n}, then the displacements of cars 1,2,…,61,2,\ldots,6 are 0,0,1,0,0,40,0,1,0,0,4, respectively.

Definition 2.7.

For a positive integer ℓ≤n\ell\leq n, we say that α\alpha is an ℓ\ell-interval parking function if maxdisp⁡(α)≤ℓ\maxdisp(\alpha)\leq\ell. The set of ℓ\ell-interval parking functions of length nn is denoted IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell). In the case ℓ=1\ell=1, we call α\alpha a unit interval parking function and write UPFn=IPFn⁡(1)\UPF_{n}=\IPF_{n}(1).

Example 2.8.

We can give exact formulas for |IPFn⁡(ℓ)||\IPF_{n}(\ell)| in some extreme cases.

  • ℓ=n−1\ell=n-1:

    Every α∈PFn\alpha\in\PF_{n} satisfies maxdisp⁡(α)≤n−1\maxdisp(\alpha)\leq n-1, so

    |IPFn⁡(n−1)|=|PFn|=(n+1)n−1.|\IPF_{n}(n-1)|=|\PF_{n}|=(n+1)^{n-1}.
  • ℓ=n−2\ell=n-2:

    Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈PFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\PF_{n}. Then maxdisp⁡(α)=n−1\maxdisp(\alpha)=n-1 if and only if the car that parks in spot nn preferred spot 1. This can happen only if (i) that car was the last to park and (ii) the first n−1n-1 cars parked in the first n−1n-1 spots. Equivalently, an=1a_{n}=1 and (a1,a2,…,an−1)∈PFn−1(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n-1})\in\PF_{n-1}. Therefore,

    |IPFn⁡(n−2)|\displaystyle|\IPF_{n}(n-2)| =|PFn|−|{α∈PFn:maxdisp⁡(α)=n−1}|=(n+1)n−1−nn−2.\displaystyle=|\PF_{n}|-|\{\alpha\in\PF_{n}\colon\maxdisp(\alpha)=n-1\}|=(n+1)^{n-1}-n^{n-2}.
  • ℓ=1\ell=1:

    The parking functions α\alpha with maxdisp⁡(α)=1\maxdisp(\alpha)=1 are precisely the unit interval parking functions. Therefore,

    |IPFn⁡(1)|=|UPFn|=Fubn,|\IPF_{n}(1)|=|\UPF_{n}|=\Fub_{n},

    where Fubn\Fub_{n} is the number of ordered set partitions of [n][n] (see Remark 2.12 below).

  • ℓ=0\ell=0:

    The parking functions α\alpha with maxdisp⁡(α)=0\maxdisp(\alpha)=0 are precisely the permutations. Therefore,

    |IPFn⁡(0)|=n!.|\IPF_{n}(0)|=n!.

It is immediate from the rearrangement criterion that any rearrangement of a parking function is a parking function. The same is not true for ℓ\ell-parking functions because maximum displacement may change under rearrangement. For instance, maxdisp⁡(112)=1\maxdisp(112)=1 but maxdisp⁡(121)=2\maxdisp(121)=2. On the other hand, a weaker result holds for all ℓ\ell, as we prove later (Proposition 3.5).

2.2. Block structure of unit interval parking functions

In [5], it was proved that unit interval parking functions are characterized by a tightly controlled block structure, as we now explain.

Definition 2.9.

A tuple β=(b1,b2,…,bn)∈[n]n\beta=(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n})\in[n]^{n} is called a block word if bi∈{i,i−1}b_{i}\in\{i,i-1\} for each ii (so in particular, b1=1b_{1}=1). When we write a block word, we place a separator before each bib_{i} such that bi=i>1b_{i}=i>1. The maximal subwords between separators are called blocks. Note that a block word is determined by the ordered list of lengths of its blocks.

For example, the block words of length 3 are 112112, 11|311\mid 3, 1|221\mid 22, 1​∣2∣​31\mid 2\mid 3.

We now reformulate the characterization of unit interval parking functions based on their block structure.

Theorem 2.10 ([5, Theorem 2.9]).

Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈UPFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\UPF_{n} and α↑=(a1′,a2′,…,an′)\alpha^{\uparrow}=(a^{\prime}_{1},a^{\prime}_{2},\dots,a^{\prime}_{n}). Then,

  1. (1)

    The increasing rearrangement α↑\alpha^{\uparrow} is a block word. If α↑=π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πm\alpha^{\uparrow}=\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{m}, we refer to the collection of πj\pi_{j}’s as the block structure of α\alpha.

  2. (2)

    The entries in each block appear in increasing order in α\alpha. That is, α\alpha is a shuffle of its blocks.

  3. (3)

    Given a block word β\beta, every shuffle of its blocks is a unit interval parking function. Therefore,

    |{α∈UPFn:α↑=β}|=(n|π1|,|π2|,…,|πm|).|\{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}\colon\alpha^{\uparrow}=\beta\}|=\binom{n}{|\pi_{1}|,|\pi_{2}|,\ldots,|\pi_{m}|}.

Next we state a bijection between the set of unit interval parking functions of length nn with mm blocks and the set of surjective functions from [n][n] to [m][m].

Corollary 2.11.

Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈UPFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\UPF_{n} have block structure π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πm\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{m}. For each i∈[n]i\in[n], let s⁡(i)s(i) be the index of the block to which aia_{i} belongs. Thus, ss is a surjective function [n]→[m][n]\to[m] (equivalently, an ordered partition of [n][n] into mm nonempty blocks). Then the map sending α↦s\alpha\mapsto s is a bijection

{α∈UPFn:α has m blocks}→{surjective functions [n]→[m]}.\{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}\colon\alpha\text{ has $m$ blocks}\}\to\{\text{surjective functions }[n]\to[m]\}.
Remark 2.12.

A surjective function [n]→[m][n]\to[m] can be regarded as an ordered set partition of [n][n] with mm nonempty blocks. In particular, the number of unit interval parking functions of length nn equals the Fubini number Fubn\Fub_{n} of ordered set partitions of [n][n], as observed by Hadaway [17]. The Fubini numbers are sequence #A000670 in [18]. We obtain a new proof this fact following Theorem 4.4.

Example 2.13.

Let α=(8,1,5,5,1,2,4,7)∈UPF8\alpha=(8,1,5,5,1,2,4,7)\in\UPF_{8}. Then the block structure is α↑=112​∣4​∣55∣​7∣​8\alpha^{\uparrow}=112\mid 4\mid 55\mid 7\mid 8, and the corresponding element of [5]8[5]^{8}, as in Corollary 2.11, is s=51331124s=51331124.

Block structure appears to be unique to the case ℓ=1\ell=1; no result analogous to Theorem 2.10 is known for ℓ\ell-interval parking functions when ℓ>1\ell>1. We state this as an open problem in Section 6.

2.3. Permutation statistics

Let w=w1⋯wn∈ℕnw=w_{1}\cdots w_{n}\in\mathbb{N}^{n} be a sequence of positive integers. An inversion of ww is a pair of indices (i,j)(i,j) such that 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n and wi>wjw_{i}>w_{j}. We let Inv⁡(w)\Inv(w) be the set of inversions of ww and let inv⁡(w)=|Inv⁡(w)|\inv(w)=|\Inv(w)|. A descent is a position i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1] such that wi>wi+1w_{i}>w_{i+1}. We let Des⁡(w)\Des(w) be the set of descents of ww and let des⁡(w)=|Des⁡(w)|\des(w)=|\Des(w)|. The major index of ww is

maj⁡(w)=∑i∈Des⁡(w)i.\maj(w)=\sum_{i\in\Des(w)}i.

By a bijection of Foata [20, 11] that we describe in detail in Section 3, inversions and major index are equidistributed as statistics on the set of permutations, meaning that there are as many permutations w∈𝔖nw\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} with inv⁡(w)=j\inv(w)=j as there are with maj⁡(w)=j\maj(w)=j, for each nonnegative integer jj. More generally, inversions and major index are equidistributed on any set of words W⊆ℕnW\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{n} satisfying the property that if w∈Ww\in W and uu is a rearrangement of ww, then u∈Wu\in W [12]. Hence, inversions and major index are equidistributed on the set of parking functions. In Section 3, we completely characterize the pairs (n,ℓ)(n,\ell) such that inversions and major index are equidistributed on IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell).

It is immediate from the definition that inv⁡(σ)=inv⁡(σ−1)\inv(\sigma)=\inv(\sigma^{-1}) for every permutation σ\sigma. For a surjective function s:[n]→[m]s:[n]\to[m], let Inv⁡(s)=Inv⁡(w)\Inv(s)=\Inv(w), where w=w1⋯wnw=w_{1}\cdots w_{n} is defined as wi=s⁡(i)w_{i}=s(i) for each ∈[n]\in[n]. The following result asserts that inversions of unit interval parking functions can be computed as inversions of permutations or surjective functions.

Lemma 2.14.

Let α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n} with corresponding surjective function ss. Then Inv⁡(α)=Inv⁡(spotα)=Inv⁡(s)\Inv(\alpha)=\Inv(\spot_{\alpha})=\Inv(s).

Proof.

Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈UPFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\UPF_{n} and let (i,j)(i,j) be an inversion of spotα\spot_{\alpha}. That is, car ii arrives earlier than car jj and parks to the the right of car jj. It follows that ai>aja_{i}>a_{j}, so (i,j)∈Inv⁡(α)(i,j)\in\Inv(\alpha).

Now let (i,j)(i,j) be an inversion of α\alpha. That is, ai>aja_{i}>a_{j} and i<ji<j. Since α\alpha is a UPF, spotα⁡(j)≤aj+1≤ai≤spotα⁡(i)\spot_{\alpha}(j)\leq a_{j}+1\leq a_{i}\leq\spot_{\alpha}(i). Thus,every inversion of α\alpha is an inversion of spotα\spot_{\alpha}.

For the second equality, by Part (b) of Theorem 2.10, we have that for all i<ji<j, ai>aja_{i}>a_{j} if and only if s⁡(i)>s⁡(j)s(i)>s(j). Hence, the claim follows. ∎

An ascent of a word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n} is a position i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1] such that wi<wi+1w_{i}<w_{i+1}. We let Asc⁡(w)\Asc(w) be the set of ascents of ww and set asc⁡(w)=|Asc⁡(w)|\asc(w)=|\Asc(w)|. It is known [23, Exercise 1.133a] that

(1) ∑σ∈𝔖n2asc⁡(σ)=Fubn=|UPFn|.\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}2^{\asc(\sigma)}=\Fub_{n}=|\UPF_{n}|.

We obtain a more refined enumerative result in Theorem 4.4.

3. Foata invariance and inv-maj equidistribution

In this section, we prove that a classical bijection of Foata [13] preserves the classes of ℓ\ell-interval parking functions for ℓ∈{1,2,n−2,n−1}\ell\in\{1,2,n-2,n-1\}, from which it follows that the inversion and major index statistics are equidistributed on each of these classes.

Theorem 3.1.

Let 1≤ℓ<n1\leq\ell<n, and let IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell) denote the class of ℓ\ell-interval parking functions of length nn.

  • •

    If ℓ∈{1,2,n−2,n−1}\ell\in\{1,2,n-2,n-1\}, then the Foata transform restricts to a bijection IPFn⁡(ℓ)→IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell)\to\IPF_{n}(\ell), and consequently the inversion and major index statistics are equidistributed on IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell), i.e.,

    ∑p∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)tinv⁡(p)=∑p∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)tmaj⁡(p).\sum_{p\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}t^{\inv(p)}=\sum_{p\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}t^{\maj(p)}.
  • •

    If ℓ∉{1,2,n−2,n−1}\ell\not\in\{1,2,n-2,n-1\}, then inversion and major index are not equidistributed on IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell), so the Foata transform cannot be a bijection IPFn⁡(ℓ)→IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell)\to\IPF_{n}(\ell).

The proof spans several cases, which we order by increasing difficulty.

  • •

    ℓ=n−2\ell=n-2: Proposition 3.7

  • •

    3≤ℓ≤n−33\leq\ell\leq n-3: Proposition 3.8

  • •

    ℓ=1\ell=1: Proposition 3.9

  • •

    ℓ=2\ell=2: Proposition 3.10

3.1. The Foata transform on words

We begin by describing Foata’s bijection [13] and its relevant properties.

Definition 3.2 ([13]).

The Foata transform is the function FF defined inductively on words w=w1⋯wnw=w_{1}\cdots w_{n} as follows.

  • •

    For n=1n=1, we set F⁡(w)=wF(w)=w.

  • •

    For n>1n>1, the image F⁡(w)F(w) is defined as follows. Let w′=F(w1⋯wn−1)=w1′⋯wn−1′w^{\prime}=F(w_{1}\cdots w_{n-1})=w^{\prime}_{1}\cdots w^{\prime}_{n-1}.

    • –

      Place a separator before w1w_{1}

    • –

      If wn≥wn−1′w_{n}\geq w^{\prime}_{n-1}, then place a separator after every wi′w^{\prime}_{i} such that wn≥wi′w_{n}\geq w^{\prime}_{i}.

    • –

      If wn<wn−1′w_{n}<w^{\prime}_{n-1}, then place a separator after every wi′w^{\prime}_{i} such that wn<wi′w_{n}<w^{\prime}_{i}.

  • •

    Cycle each segment (i.e., each maximal subword between consecutive separators) by moving its rightmost entry to the start.

  • •

    Finally, append wnw_{n}. The result is F⁡(w)F(w).

Example 3.3.

We show how to compute F⁡(w)F(w) for w=315312w=315312. Each line is showing how you compute F(w1⋯wi)F(w_{1}\cdots w_{i}) by first placing the separators to form the segments, and then the cycling segments and placing wiw_{i} on the end.

3|3|→31|3|1|→315|315|→5313|5|​3​|13|→53311|5331|1|→153312=F⁡(w)\begin{array}[]{lclc}3&\\ |3|&\rightarrow&31\\ |3|1|&\rightarrow&315\\ |315|&\rightarrow&5313\\ |5|3|13|&\rightarrow&53311\\ |5331|1|&\rightarrow&153312&=F(w)\end{array}

Foata [13] proved that FF is a bijection such that inv⁡(F⁡(w))=maj⁡(w)\inv(F(w))=\maj(w) for all words ww. This implies that the inversion number and major index are equidistributed for permutations (which are 00-interval parking functions), i.e.,

(2) ∑w∈𝔖nqinv⁡(w)=∑w∈𝔖nqmaj⁡(w).\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}q^{\inv(w)}=\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}q^{\maj(w)}.

Equidistribution had been proved previously by MacMahon [20], but the Foata transform gave the first combinatorial proof. For more detail, see [23, pp. 41–43].

It is immediate from the definition of FF that it preserves the content of a word, i.e., the number of occurrences of each letter. In particular, it preserves the class of parking functions (which are (n−1)(n-1)-interval parking functions). Moreover, the definition of FF also implies that for each ii, the “partial Foata transform” FiF_{i} defined by Fi(w)=F(w1⋯wi)wi+1⋯wnF_{i}(w)=F(w_{1}\cdots w_{i})w_{i+1}\cdots w_{n} is also a bijection.

The motivating question of this section is: When does the Foata transform preserve the class of ℓ\ell-interval parking functions of length nn? When the answer is positive, equidistribution of inversion number and major index for that class follows immediately.

3.2. Permuting parking functions

In this section, we need to compare different parking functions related by permutations (specifically, by partial Foata transforms) and keep track of the effects on individual cars. Accordingly, we assign each car a permanent unique identifier (its “license plate”, so to speak) and denote a parking function p=(p1,…,pn)p=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n}) by a two-line array

p=(C1⋯Cnp1⋯pn)p=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}C_{1}&\cdots&C_{n}\\ p_{1}&\cdots&p_{n}\end{array}\right)

in which CiC_{i} means the car with license plate ii; pip_{i} is its preference; and the order of columns indicates the order with which cars enter the parking lot.

For example, let pp be the parking function 112, in which the iith car to enter has license plate ii, and let qq be the parking function obtained by interchanging the second and third cars. In our notation, we write

p=(C1C2C3112),q=(C1C3C2121),p=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}C_{1}&C_{2}&C_{3}\\ 1&1&2\end{array}\right),\qquad q=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}C_{1}&C_{3}&C_{2}\\ 1&2&1\end{array}\right),

from which it is easy to compare the outcomes of pp and qq.

We write spotp⁡(Ci)\spot_{p}(C_{i}) for the spot in which car CiC_{i} parks with respect to pp, and define dispp⁡(Ci)=spotp⁡(Ci)−pi\disp_{p}(C_{i})=\spot_{p}(C_{i})-p_{i}. For example, if pp is the parking function

p=(C1C2C3C4C5C6111143)p=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccccc}C_{1}&C_{2}&C_{3}&C_{4}&C_{5}&C_{6}\\ 1&1&1&1&4&3\end{array}\right)

then its Foata transform is

r=F⁡(p)=(C5C1C2C3C4C6411113).r=F(p)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccccc}C_{5}&C_{1}&C_{2}&C_{3}&C_{4}&C_{6}\\ 4&1&1&1&1&3\end{array}\right).

We can see for example that spotr⁡(C4)=5\spot_{r}(C_{4})=5 and dispr⁡(C4)=5−1=4\disp_{r}(C_{4})=5-1=4. Recall that a parking function pp is an ℓ\ell-interval parking function if and only if maxi⁡{dispp⁡(Ci)}≤ℓ\max_{i}\{\disp_{p}(C_{i})\}\leq\ell.

Lemma 3.4 (Interval Rearrangement).

Let pp be a parking function of length nn. Partition [n][n] into intervals B1,…,BkB_{1},\dots,B_{k}, and let q=(pw−1​(1),…,pw−1​(n))q=(p_{w^{-1}(1)},\dots,p_{w^{-1}(n)}) for some w∈𝔖B1×⋯×𝔖Bkw\in\mathfrak{S}_{B_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mathfrak{S}_{B_{k}}. Then for each i∈[k]i\in[k], we have

{spotp⁡(j):j∈Bi}={spotq⁡(j):j∈Bi}.\{\spot_{p}(j)\colon j\in B_{i}\}=\{\spot_{q}(j)\colon j\in B_{i}\}.

This fact may be known, but we have not found it in the literature, so we give a short proof.

Proof.

Let

p=(C1⋯Cnp1⋯pn).p=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}C_{1}&\cdots&C_{n}\\ p_{1}&\cdots&p_{n}\end{array}\right).

The permutation ww can be factored as a product of adjacent transpositions, each one belonging to some 𝔖Bj\mathfrak{S}_{B_{j}}, so it suffices to show that interchanging the order of two adjacent cars either preserves or swaps their outcomes. Let

q=(C1⋯Ci−1Ci+1CiCi+2⋯Cnp1⋯pi−1pi+1pipi+2⋯pn)q=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccccc}C_{1}&\cdots&C_{i-1}&C_{i+1}&C_{i}&C_{i+2}\cdots&C_{n}\\ p_{1}&\cdots&p_{i-1}&p_{i+1}&p_{i}&p_{i+2}\cdots&p_{n}\end{array}\right)

for some ii and suppose that SS is the set of parking spots available after cars C1,…,Ci−1C_{1},\dots,C_{i-1} park in pp. Set pi=up_{i}=u and pi+1=vp_{i+1}=v. Then, we have

a:=spotp⁡(Ci)=min⁡{s∈S:s≥u},b:=spotp⁡(Ci+1)=min⁡{s∈S∖a:s≥v}a:=\spot_{p}(C_{i})=\min\{s\in S\colon s\geq u\},\quad b:=\spot_{p}(C_{i+1})=\min\{s\in S\setminus a\colon s\geq v\}

and if q=(p1,…,pi+1,pi,…,pn)q=(p_{1},\dots,p_{i+1},p_{i},\dots,p_{n}), we have

y:=spotq⁡(Ci+1)=min⁡{s∈S:s≥v},z:=spotq⁡(Ci)=min⁡{s∈S∖y:s≥u}.y:=\spot_{q}(C_{i+1})=\min\{s\in S\colon s\geq v\},\quad z:=\spot_{q}(C_{i})=\min\{s\in S\setminus y\colon s\geq u\}.

If u=vu=v then evidently a=ya=y and b=zb=z. Without loss of generality, assume u<vu<v.

Evidently u≤a≤zu\leq a\leq z and v≤y≤bv\leq y\leq b. If (a,y)=(z,b)(a,y)=(z,b) then we are done. Otherwise, either a<za<z or y<by<b. In the first case, the definitions of aa and zz imply that y=ay=a, from which it follows that u,u+1,…,v−1∉Su,u+1,\dots,v-1\not\in S, and these two conditions together imply z=bz=b. A similar argument shows that y<by<b implies (y,z)=(a,b)(y,z)=(a,b). ∎

Lemma 3.4 generalizes easily from parking functions to parking completions (see [1]). One useful consequence is the following.

Proposition 3.5.

Suppose p,qp,q are two parking functions obtained by switching two adjacent cars, as follows:

p=(⋯C1C2⋯⋯x1x2⋯),q=(⋯C2C1⋯⋯x2x1⋯),p=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\cdots&C_{1}&C_{2}&\cdots\\ \cdots&x_{1}&x_{2}&\cdots\end{array}\right),\qquad q=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\cdots&C_{2}&C_{1}&\cdots\\ \cdots&x_{2}&x_{1}&\cdots\end{array}\right),

with x1>x2x_{1}>x_{2}. Then maxdisp⁡(p)≥maxdisp⁡(q)\maxdisp(p)\geq\maxdisp(q). In particular, the increasing rearrangement of every ℓ\ell-interval parking function is an ℓ\ell-interval parking function.

Proof.

By interval rearrangement (Lemma 3.4), the sets {spotp⁡(C1),spotp⁡(C2)}\{\spot_{p}(C_{1}),\spot_{p}(C_{2})\} and {spotq⁡(C1),spotq⁡(C2)}\{\spot_{q}(C_{1}),\spot_{q}(C_{2})\} are equal, say to {a,b}\{a,b\}, where a<ba<b. If spotp⁡(C1)=spotq⁡(C1)\spot_{p}(C_{1})=\spot_{q}(C_{1}) and spotp⁡(C2)=spotq⁡(C2)\spot_{p}(C_{2})=\spot_{q}(C_{2}), then maxdisp⁡(p)=maxdisp⁡(q)\maxdisp(p)=\maxdisp(q). Otherwise, we have without loss of generality

a=spotp⁡(C1)=spotq⁡(C2)<spotp⁡(C2)=spotq⁡(C1)=b.a=\spot_{p}(C_{1})=\spot_{q}(C_{2})<\spot_{p}(C_{2})=\spot_{q}(C_{1})=b.

In particular, b>a≥x1>x2b>a\geq x_{1}>x_{2}, and

max⁡(dispp⁡(C1),dispp⁡(C2))=max⁡(a−x1,b−x2)\displaystyle\max(\disp_{p}(C_{1}),\disp_{p}(C_{2}))=\max(a-x_{1},b-x_{2})
>\displaystyle> max⁡(dispq⁡(C1),dispq⁡(C2))=max⁡(b−x1,a−x2).\displaystyle\max(\disp_{q}(C_{1}),\disp_{q}(C_{2}))=\max(b-x_{1},a-x_{2}).

Thus, replacing pp with qq can only decrease the maximum displacement, as claimed. Iterating this argument shows that bubble-sorting (taking a ℓ\ell-interval parking function and sorting the smallest element to position 1, then the second smallest to position 2, etc.) produces an ℓ\ell-interval parking function. ∎

Lemma 3.6 (Reserved Spot Lemma).

For 1≤j<k≤n1\leq j<k\leq n, let

p=(C1⋯Cnp1⋯pn)andq=(C1⋯Cj−1CkCj⋯Ck−1Ck+1⋯Cnp1⋯pj−1pkpj⋯pk−1pk+1⋯pn)p=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}C_{1}&\cdots&C_{n}\\ p_{1}&\cdots&p_{n}\end{array}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad q=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc|cccc|ccc}C_{1}&\cdots&C_{j-1}&C_{k}&C_{j}&\cdots&C_{k-1}&C_{k+1}&\cdots&C_{n}\\ p_{1}&\cdots&p_{j-1}&p_{k}&p_{j}&\cdots&p_{k-1}&p_{k+1}&\cdots&p_{n}\end{array}\right)

be parking functions (where the bars are included merely for clarity), and suppose that spotp⁡(Ck)=spotq⁡(Ck)\spot_{p}(C_{k})=\spot_{q}(C_{k}). Then spotp⁡(Ci)=spotq⁡(Ci)\spot_{p}(C_{i})=\spot_{q}(C_{i}) for all i∈[n]i\in[n].

Proof.

The name of the lemma is also its proof: imagine that in pp, right after car Cj−1C_{j-1} parks, driver CkC_{k} runs up and puts a cone in spot pkp_{k} to reserve it (even if it is not their preferred spot). Since car CkC_{k} got to park in spot pkp_{k} anyway, this has no impact on the outcome of pp. On the other hand, “reserving” spot pkp_{k} after car Cj−1C_{j-1} parks is equivalent to letting car CkC_{k} park there, so the outcome of doing so must be the same as the outcome of qq. ∎

3.3. Proof of Theorem 3.1

We begin with the easiest cases, showing that the Foata transform is a bijection when ℓ=n−2\ell=n-2, but not when 3≤ℓ≤n−33\leq\ell\leq n-3.

Proposition 3.7.

For all n≥3n\geq 3, the Foata transform restricts to a bijection IPFn⁡(n−2)→IPFn⁡(n−2)\IPF_{n}(n-2)\to\IPF_{n}(n-2).

Proof.

A parking function pp of length nn fails to be an (n−2)(n-2)-parking function precisely when some car has displacement n−1n-1. That car must be the last to park, must prefer spot 1, and must park in spot nn, which implies that p^=(p1,…,pn−1)\hat{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n-1}) is a parking function of length n−1n-1. Since pn=1p_{n}=1, it follows that FF fixes the last digit of pp and permutes the entries of p^\hat{p}. It follows that FF restricts to a bijection PFn∖IPFn⁡(n−2)→PFn∖IPFn⁡(n−2)\PF_{n}\setminus\IPF_{n}(n-2)\to\PF_{n}\setminus\IPF_{n}(n-2), hence also to a bijection IPFn⁡(n−2)→IPFn⁡(n−2)\IPF_{n}(n-2)\to\IPF_{n}(n-2). ∎

Proposition 3.8.

For n≥6n\geq 6 and 3≤ℓ≤n−33\leq\ell\leq n-3, the statistics inv\inv and maj\maj are not equidistributed on IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell).

Proof.

Let ℐn,ℓ={p∈IPFn⁡(ℓ):inv⁡(p)=1}\mathcal{I}_{n,\ell}=\{p\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)\colon\inv(p)=1\} and ℳn,ℓ={p∈IPFn⁡(ℓ):maj⁡(p)=1}\mathcal{M}_{n,\ell}=\{p\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)\colon\maj(p)=1\}. We show that |ℳn,ℓ|<|ℐn,ℓ||\mathcal{M}_{n,\ell}|<|\mathcal{I}_{n,\ell}|. To do so, define

𝒫n,ℓI\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I} ={(α,i)∈IPFn↑⁡(ℓ)×[n−1]:(I1)ai<ai+1, and (I2)either ai+1>i or dispα⁡(Ci)≤ℓ−1},\displaystyle=\left\{(\alpha,i)\in\IPF_{n}^{\uparrow}(\ell)\times[n-1]\colon\begin{array}[]{l}\textbf{(I1)}\ \ a_{i}<a_{i+1},\text{ and }\\ \textbf{(I2)}\ \ \text{either $a_{i+1}>i$ or $\disp_{\alpha}(C_{i})\leq\ell-1$}\end{array}\right\},
𝒫n,ℓM\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M} ={(α,i)∈IPFn↑⁡(ℓ)×[n−1]:(M1)ai<ai+1, and (M2)for all j∈[n], if ai+1≤j≤i, then dispα⁡(Cj)≤ℓ−1}.\displaystyle=\left\{(\alpha,i)\in\IPF_{n}^{\uparrow}(\ell)\times[n-1]\colon\begin{array}[]{l}\textbf{(M1)}\ \ a_{i}<a_{i+1},\text{ and }\\ \textbf{(M2)}\ \ \text{for all $j\in[n]$, if $a_{i+1}\leq j\leq i$, then $\disp_{\alpha}(C_{j})\leq\ell-1$}\end{array}\right\}.

Our plan is to define bijections κ:𝒫n,ℓI→ℐn,ℓ\kappa:\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I}\to\mathcal{I}_{n,\ell} and λ:𝒫n,ℓM→ℳn,ℓ\lambda:\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}\to\mathcal{M}_{n,\ell}, then to show that 𝒫n,ℓI⊋𝒫n,ℓM\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I}\supsetneq\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}.

First, given a pair (α,i)∈𝒫n,ℓI(\alpha,i)\in\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I}, let β=κ⁡(α,i)\beta=\kappa(\alpha,i) be the parking function obtained by swapping aia_{i} and ai+1a_{i+1}. Since α=α↑\alpha=\alpha^{\uparrow}, it follows that β\beta is a parking function with one inversion, and α\alpha can be recovered from β\beta as its increasing rearrangement.

By interval rearrangement (Lemma 3.4), every car has the same outcome in β\beta as it does in α\alpha, except that CiC_{i} and Ci+1C_{i+1} may switch places. Since α=α↑\alpha=\alpha^{\uparrow}, the two parking spots in question are ii and i+1i+1. There are two possibilities:

  • •

    If ai+1=i+1a_{i+1}=i+1, then spotβ⁡(Cj)=spotα⁡(Cj)\spot_{\beta}(C_{j})=\spot_{\alpha}(C_{j}) for every j∈[n]j\in[n], and it follows that β∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)\beta\in\IPF_{n}(\ell).

  • •

    If ai+1≤ia_{i+1}\leq i, then (spotβ⁡(Ci),spotβ⁡(Ci+1))=(spotα⁡(Ci+1),spotα⁡(Ci))=(i+1,i)(\spot_{\beta}(C_{i}),\spot_{\beta}(C_{i+1}))=(\spot_{\alpha}(C_{i+1}),\spot_{\alpha}(C_{i}))=(i+1,i). Thus, we have a injective map κ:𝒫n,ℓI→ℐn,ℓ\kappa:\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I}\to\mathcal{I}_{n,\ell}. For surjectivity, observe that if β∈ℐn,ℓ\beta\in\mathcal{I}_{n,\ell} has a unique inversion bi>bi+1b_{i}>b_{i+1}, then α=β↑∈IPFn↑⁡(ℓ)\alpha=\beta^{\uparrow}\in\IPF_{n}^{\uparrow}(\ell) by Proposition 3.5, and the same case argument shows that (α,i)∈𝒫n,ℓI(\alpha,i)\in\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I}.

Second, given a pair (α,i)∈𝒫n,ℓM(\alpha,i)\in\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}, let β=λ⁡(α,i)\beta=\lambda(\alpha,i) be the parking function obtained by moving ai+1a_{i+1} to the front. Similarly to the first case, β\beta is a parking function with major index 1, and α=β↑\alpha=\beta^{\uparrow}.

spotβ⁡(Cj)={ai+1 if ​j=i+1,spotα⁡(Cj) if ​j≤i​ and ​spotα⁡(Cj)<ai+1,spotα⁡(Cj)+1 if ​j≤i​ and ​spotα⁡(Cj)≥ai+1,\spot_{\beta}(C_{j})=\begin{cases}a_{i+1}&\text{ if }j=i+1,\\ \spot_{\alpha}(C_{j})&\text{ if }j\leq i\text{ and }\spot_{\alpha}(C_{j})<a_{i+1},\\ \spot_{\alpha}(C_{j})+1&\text{ if }j\leq i\text{ and }\spot_{\alpha}(C_{j})\geq a_{i+1},\end{cases}

and

dispβ⁡(Cj)={0 if ​j=i+1,dispα⁡(Cj) if ​j≤i​ and ​spotα⁡(Cj)<ai+1,dispα⁡(Cj)+1 if ​j≤i​ and ​spotα⁡(Cj)≥ai+1,={0 if ​j=i+1,dispα⁡(Cj) if ​j<ai+1,dispα⁡(Cj)+1 if ​ai+1≤j≤i.\disp_{\beta}(C_{j})=\begin{cases}0&\text{ if }j=i+1,\\ \disp_{\alpha}(C_{j})&\text{ if }j\leq i\text{ and }\spot_{\alpha}(C_{j})<a_{i+1},\\ \disp_{\alpha}(C_{j})+1&\text{ if }j\leq i\text{ and }\spot_{\alpha}(C_{j})\geq a_{i+1},\end{cases}=\begin{cases}0&\text{ if }j=i+1,\\ \disp_{\alpha}(C_{j})&\text{ if }j<a_{i+1},\\ \disp_{\alpha}(C_{j})+1&\text{ if }a_{i+1}\leq j\leq i.\end{cases}

From this and condition (M2) in the definition of 𝒫n,ℓM\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}, we can conclude that β\beta has maximum displacement at most ℓ\ell, hence belongs to ℳn,ℓ\mathcal{M}_{n,\ell}.

Thus, we have an injective map λ:𝒫n,ℓM→ℳn,ℓ\lambda:\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}\to\mathcal{M}_{n,\ell}. To see that λ\lambda is a surjection, let β∈ℳn,ℓ\beta\in\mathcal{M}_{n,\ell}. Then α=β↑\alpha=\beta^{\uparrow} has the form

where ii is the greatest index such that b1>bi+1b_{1}>b_{i+1}. Then α∈IPFn↑⁡(ℓ)\alpha\in\IPF_{n}^{\uparrow}(\ell) by Proposition 3.5, and again the calculation above shows that (α,i)∈𝒫n,ℓM(\alpha,i)\in\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}.

Third, it is immediate from their definitions that 𝒫n,ℓI⊇𝒫n,ℓM\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I}\supseteq\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}. To prove that containment is strict, consider the parking function

p=(1,…,1⏟ℓ+1​ copies,ℓ+1,ℓ,ℓ+4,ℓ+5,…,n)∈ℐn,ℓp=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{\ell+1\mbox{ copies}},\ell+1,\ell,\ell+4,\ell+5,\dots,n)\in\mathcal{I}_{n,\ell}

(recall that n≥6n\geq 6 and 3≤ℓ≤n−33\leq\ell\leq n-3). Then κ−1​(p)=(α,ℓ+2)\kappa^{-1}(p)=(\alpha,\ell+2), where

α=(1,…,1⏟ℓ+1​ copies,ℓ,ℓ+1,ℓ+4,ℓ+5,…,n).\alpha=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{\ell+1\mbox{ copies}},\ell,\ell+1,\ell+4,\ell+5,\dots,n).

Thus,(α,ℓ+2)∈𝒫n,ℓI(\alpha,\ell+2)\in\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{I}. However, setting i=ℓ+2i=\ell+2 and j=ℓ+1j=\ell+1, we have

ai+1=ℓ+1≤j≤i,butdispα⁡(Cj)=(ℓ+1)−aℓ+1=(ℓ+1)−1=ℓ.a_{i+1}=\ell+1\leq j\leq i,\quad\text{but}\quad\disp_{\alpha}(C_{j})=(\ell+1)-a_{\ell+1}=(\ell+1)-1=\ell.

So condition (M2) fails and (α,ℓ+2)∉𝒫n,ℓM(\alpha,\ell+2)\notin\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}^{M}, proving strict containment as desired. ∎

We next consider the case ℓ=1\ell=1.

Proposition 3.9.

For all n≥1n\geq 1, the Foata transform restricts to a bijection UPFn→UPFn\UPF_{n}\to\UPF_{n}.

Proof.

We begin by analyzing what generally happens to a UPF if we cycle a segment. Let q∈UPFnq\in\UPF_{n}, and let rr be the parking function obtained by cycling a single interval [a,b][a,b]:

q=(⋯Ca⋯Cb⋯⋯qa⋯qb⋯)→r=(⋯CbCa⋯Cb−1⋯⋯qbqa⋯qb−1⋯).q=\left(\begin{array}[]{c|ccc|c}\cdots&C_{a}&\cdots&C_{b}&\cdots\\ \cdots&q_{a}&\cdots&q_{b}&\cdots\end{array}\right)\ \quad\to\quad r=\left(\begin{array}[]{c|cccc|c}\cdots&C_{b}&C_{a}&\cdots&C_{b-1}&\cdots\\ \cdots&q_{b}&q_{a}&\cdots&q_{b-1}&\cdots\end{array}\right).

Here the bars are included for clarity. Note that spotr⁡(Cb)≤spotq⁡(Cb)\spot_{r}(C_{b})\leq\spot_{q}(C_{b}) because passing from qq to rr moves CbC_{b} toward the front of the queue. We show that dispr⁡(Ci)≤2\disp_{r}(C_{i})\leq 2 for each i∈[a,b].i\in[a,b].

If spotr⁡(Cb)=spotq⁡(Cb)\spot_{r}(C_{b})=\spot_{q}(C_{b}), then the Reserved Spot Lemma (Lemma 3.6) implies that all outcomes are preserved, so r∈UPFnr\in\UPF_{n}. Accordingly, we assume henceforth that spotr⁡(Cb)<spotq⁡(Cb)\spot_{r}(C_{b})<\spot_{q}(C_{b}). Since qq is a unit interval parking function, we have

0≤dispr⁡(Cb)=spotr⁡(Cb)−qb<spotq⁡(Cb)−qb=dispq⁡(Cb)≤10\leq\disp_{r}(C_{b})=\spot_{r}(C_{b})-q_{b}<\spot_{q}(C_{b})-q_{b}=\disp_{q}(C_{b})\leq 1

so the two inequalities are both actually equalities. In particular,

(3) spotr⁡(Cb)=qbandspotq⁡(Cb)=qb+1.\spot_{r}(C_{b})=q_{b}\quad\text{and}\quad\spot_{q}(C_{b})=q_{b}+1.

∑i=abspotq⁡(Ci)\displaystyle\sum_{i=a}^{b}\spot_{q}(C_{i}) =∑i=abspotr⁡(Ci)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=a}^{b}\spot_{r}(C_{i})
so
∑i=abdispq⁡(Ci)\displaystyle\sum_{i=a}^{b}\disp_{q}(C_{i}) =∑i=abdispr⁡(Ci)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=a}^{b}\disp_{r}(C_{i})
and

In the remainder of the paper, we return to the usual one-line notation for parking functions.

4. Generating functions for displacement and inversions

In this section, we study the generating function

Φn,ℓ=Φn,ℓ​(q,t)=∑α∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)qdisp⁡(α)​tinv⁡(α).\Phi_{n,\ell}=\Phi_{n,\ell}(q,t)=\sum_{\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\inv(\alpha)}.

The Foata transform FF preserves the content of a parking function and therefore its displacement. Therefore, Theorem 3.1 has the following immediate consequence.

Corollary 4.1.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and ℓ∈{0,1,2,n−2,n−1}\ell\in\{0,1,2,n-2,n-1\}. Then

Φn,ℓ=∑α∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)qdisp⁡(α)​tinv⁡(α)=∑α∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)qdisp⁡(α)​tmaj⁡(α).\Phi_{n,\ell}=\sum_{\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\inv(\alpha)}=\sum_{\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\maj(\alpha)}.

For the ℓ=0\ell=0 case (i.e. permutations), Φn,ℓ​(q,t)\Phi_{n,\ell}(q,t) has the elegant and well known formula

Φn,0​(q,t)=∏i=1n[i]q\Phi_{n,0}(q,t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}[i]_{q}

where [i]q=1+q+⋯+qm−1[i]_{q}=1+q+\dots+q^{m-1}. The polynomial Φn,0​(q,t)\Phi_{n,0}(q,t) is denoted [n]q![n]_{q}! and referred to as the “qq-factorial”.

In [6], a subset of the authors gave closed formulas for the “qq-exponential generating functions” ∑n≥0Φn,n−1​(1,q)​zn[n]q!\sum_{n\geq 0}\Phi_{n,n-1}(1,q)\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!} and ∑n≥0Φn,1​(1,q)​zn[n]q!\sum_{n\geq 0}\Phi_{n,1}(1,q)\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!} tracking inversions among all parking functions and among unit interval parking functions respectively.

We build on the approach taken by [9] in studying the specialization of Φn,n−1\Phi_{n,n-1} which only tracks displacement. There they gave a formula for Φn,n−1​(q,1)\Phi_{n,n-1}(q,1) as a sum over permutations. Using their approach, we prove a formula for Φn,ℓ​(q,1)\Phi_{n,\ell}(q,1) in Theorem 4.3 by partitioning IPFn⁡(ℓ)\IPF_{n}(\ell) into the fibers of the function 𝒞n,ℓ:IPFn⁡(ℓ)→𝔖n\Out_{n,\ell}\colon\IPF_{n}(\ell)\to\mathfrak{S}_{n} defined by 𝒞n,ℓ⁡(α)=carα\Out_{n,\ell}(\alpha)=\car_{\alpha}. Following [9], this formula can be upgraded to a (q,t)(q,t)-version tracking parking function statistics which are derived from permutation statistics. In Theorem 4.4 we use the specialization of Theorem 4.3 to obtain a particularly nice formula for Φn,1​(q,t)\Phi_{n,1}(q,t). We explore cyclic sieving phenomena for Φn,1​(q,t)\Phi_{n,1}(q,t) in Section 4.2, and in Section 4.3 we apply another “counting by fibers” technique to obtain a formula for Φn,2​(q,t)\Phi_{n,2}(q,t) as a sum over unit interval parking functions.

For the case ℓ=n−2\ell=n-2, we can write Φn,n−2\Phi_{n,n-2} in terms of displacement-inversion enumerators for (classical) parking functions. This also follows from the description of PFn∖IPFn⁡(n−2)\PF_{n}\setminus\IPF_{n}(n-2) in Example 2.8.

Corollary 4.2.

For all n≥2n\geq 2,

Φn,n−2​(q,t)\displaystyle\Phi_{n,n-2}(q,t) =Φn,n−1−(q​t)n−1​∑β∈PFn−1qdisp⁡(β)​tinv⁡(β)−ones⁡(β)\displaystyle=\Phi_{n,n-1}-(qt)^{n-1}\sum_{\beta\in\PF_{n-1}}q^{\disp(\beta)}t^{\inv(\beta)-\ones(\beta)}
=Φn,n−1−(q​t)n−1​∑β∈PFn−1qdisp⁡(β)​tmaj⁡(β)−ones⁡(β)\displaystyle=\Phi_{n,n-1}-(qt)^{n-1}\sum_{\beta\in\PF_{n-1}}q^{\disp(\beta)}t^{\maj(\beta)-\ones(\beta)}
=Φn,n−1−(q​t)n−1​∑β∈PFn−1qdisp⁡(β)​tmaj⁡(β)−lastisone⁡(β)\displaystyle=\Phi_{n,n-1}-(qt)^{n-1}\sum_{\beta\in\PF_{n-1}}q^{\disp(\beta)}t^{\maj(\beta)-\mathrm{lastisone}(\beta)}

where ones⁡(β)=|{i∈[n−1]:bi=1}|\ones(\beta)=|\{i\in[n-1]\colon b_{i}=1\}| and lastisone⁡(β)\mathrm{lastisone}(\beta) is defined to be n−1n-1 if βn−1=1\beta_{n-1}=1 and 00 otherwise.

Proof.

Recall that PFn∖IPFn⁡(n−2)\PF_{n}\setminus\IPF_{n}(n-2) is the set of parking functions β​1\beta 1 with β∈PFn−1\beta\in\PF_{n-1}. Such a parking function inherits the inversions of the β\beta and has an additional inversion for each preference of β\beta that is not equal to 1. This proves the first equation. The second equation follows by applying the Foata transform. The final equation is by noting that maj⁡(β​1)=maj⁡(β)+(n−1)−lastisone⁡(β)\maj(\beta 1)=\maj(\beta)+(n-1)-\mathrm{lastisone}(\beta). ∎

4.1. Enumeration by counting through permutations

For a permutation σ=σ1σ2⋯σn∈𝔖n\sigma=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\cdots\sigma_{n}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} and position i∈[n]i\in[n], define

(6) Lℓ​(i,σ)=min⁡(ℓ+1,i−t+1),L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)=\min(\ell+1,i-t+1),

where σt,σt+1,…,σi\sigma_{t},\sigma_{t+1},\ldots,\sigma_{i} is the longest contiguous subsequence of σ\sigma such that σk≤σi\sigma_{k}\leq\sigma_{i} for all k∈[t,i]k\in[t,i]. That is, Lℓ​(i,σ)L_{\ell}(i;\sigma) is the number of possible preferred spots for car σi\sigma_{i} that results in car σi\sigma_{i} parking in spot ii, subject to the choices of the previous cars and the constraint that the result must be an ℓ\ell-interval parking function. It follows that for all ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N} and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we have

(7) |𝒞n,ℓ−1⁡(σ)|=∏i=1nLℓ​(i,σ).|\Out_{n,\ell}^{-1}(\sigma)|=\prod_{i=1}^{n}L_{\ell}(i;\sigma).

The ℓ=n−1\ell=n-1 case of (7) is [19, Eqns. 2.1, 2.2]; see also [9, Proposition 3.1] and [24, Exercise 5.49d]. Our Ln−1​(i,σ)L_{n-1}(i;\sigma) corresponds to τi,n​(σ)\tau_{i,n}(\sigma) in [19] and to ℓ⁡(i,σ)\ell(i;\sigma) in [9].

In the case that σ=id\sigma=\id is the identity permutation, the number Lℓ​(i,id)L_{\ell}(i,\id) is either ii (if i≤ℓi\leq\ell) or ℓ+1\ell+1 (if ℓ+1≤i≤n\ell+1\leq i\leq n), so |𝒞n,ℓ−1⁡(id)|=(ℓ+1)n−ℓ⋅ℓ!|\Out_{n,\ell}^{-1}(\id)|=(\ell+1)^{n-\ell}\cdot\ell!. These numbers occur as sequence #A299504 in [18], where they count certain permutations; here, they count certain parking functions.

It follows from (7) that

(8) |IPFn⁡(ℓ)|=∑σ∈𝔖n∏i=1nLℓ​(i,σ).|\IPF_{n}(\ell)|=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}L_{\ell}(i;\sigma).

This is more efficient for explicit computation than iterating over all parking functions and picking out those with maximum displacement at most ℓ\ell. In general, we do not have a closed formula for |IPFn⁡(ℓ)||\IPF_{n}(\ell)| except in extreme cases; see Example 2.8.

In [9, Props. 5.2, 5.3], the authors provide qq-analogues of equations (7) and (8) for parking functions (as opposed to ℓ\ell-interval parking functions) using total displacement. They extend this to a (q,t)(q,t)-analogue in [9, Cor. 5.3] using permutation statistics. We can obtain a similar (q,t)(q,t)-analogue for ℓ\ell-interval parking functions.

Theorem 4.3.

Let 0≤ℓ≤n−10\leq\ell\leq n-1. For all σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we have

(9) ∑α∈𝒞n,ℓ−1⁡(σ)qdisp⁡(α)=∏i=1n[Lℓ​(i,σ)]q,\sum_{\alpha\in\Out_{n,\ell}^{-1}(\sigma)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}[L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)]_{q},

where [m]q=1+q+⋯+qm−1[m]_{q}=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}. Therefore,

(10) ∑α∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)qdisp⁡(α)​tstat⁡(carα)=∑σ∈𝔖ntstat⁡(σ)​∏i=1n[Lℓ​(i,σ)]q.\sum_{\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\mathrm{stat}(\car_{\alpha})}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}t^{\mathrm{stat}(\sigma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}[L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)]_{q}.

for any permutation statistic stat:𝔖n→ℂ\mathrm{stat}:\mathfrak{S}_{n}\to\mathbb{C}.

Proof.

Let σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} and α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈𝒞n,ℓ−1⁡(σ)\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\Out_{n,\ell}^{-1}(\sigma). For each ii, if car σi\sigma_{i} parks in spot ii, then aia_{i} must be selected from [i−Lℓ​(i,σ)+1,i][i-L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)+1,i]. Hence, for each j∈{0,…,Lℓ​(i,σ)−1}j\in\{0,\dots,L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)-1\}, the selection of ai=i−j∈[i−Lℓ​(i,σ)+1,i]a_{i}=i-j\in[i-L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)+1,i] contributes jj to the total displacement. Since [Lℓ​(i,σ)]q=1+q+⋯+qLℓ​(i,σ)−1[L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)]_{q}=1+q+\cdots+q^{L_{\ell}(i;\sigma)-1}, we obtain (9). For (10), observe that

∑α∈IPFn⁡(ℓ)qdisp⁡(α)​tstat⁡(carα)=∑σ∈𝔖n(∑α∈𝒞n,ℓ−1⁡(σ)qdisp⁡(α))​tstat⁡(σ)\sum_{\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(\ell)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\mathrm{stat}(\car_{\alpha})}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\Out_{n,\ell}^{-1}(\sigma)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}\right)t^{\mathrm{stat}(\sigma)}

and then apply (9). ∎

The ℓ=n−1\ell=n-1 case is [9, Cor. 5.3]. Also note that nothing stops us from including more variables and tracking multiple statistics at once with essentially the same formula.

In the case ℓ=1\ell=1 (unit interval parking functions), the formula of Theorem 4.3 can be written in a very nice formula in terms of classical permutation statistics. Recall from Lemma 2.14 that Inv⁡(α)=Inv⁡(spotα)\Inv(\alpha)=\Inv(\spot_{\alpha}) for α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n}. This means that for unit interval parking functions, (10) can be used to tell us about inversions, descents, and major index as computed on the parking functions (and not just their associated permutations).

Theorem 4.4.

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

(11) Φn,1​(q,t)\displaystyle\Phi_{n,1}(q,t) =∑σ∈𝔖n(1+q)asc⁡(σ)​tinv⁡(σ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(1+q)^{\asc(\sigma)}t^{\inv(\sigma)}
(12) =∑σ∈𝔖n(1+q)asc⁡(σ)​tmaj⁡(σ−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(1+q)^{\asc(\sigma)}t^{\maj(\sigma^{-1})}

Moreover,

Remark 4.5.

Setting q=−1q=-1 in Theorem 4.4 yields

since the permutation w0​(i)=n−i+1w_{0}(i)=n-i+1 is the only one with no ascents. This formula can also be proven combinatorially by constructing a sign-reversing, inversion-preserving involution on unit interval parking functions. Given α∈UPFn∖{w0}\alpha\in\UPF_{n}\setminus\{w_{0}\}, let π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πm\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{m} be its block structure (see Theorem 2.10), and let kk be the smallest index such that either (i) |πk|≥2|\pi_{k}|\geq 2, or (ii) |πk|=1|\pi_{k}|=1 and πk\pi_{k} appears earlier in α\alpha than every member of πk+1\pi_{k+1}. (The condition α≠w0\alpha\neq w_{0} implies that at least one of conditions (i), (ii) must be satisfied.) Then, define φ⁡(α)\varphi(\alpha) by modifying α\alpha as follows:

  1. (1)

    If πk=(j,j,j+1,j+2,…)\pi_{k}=(j,j,j+1,j+2,\dots), then replace the second occurrence of jj by j+1j+1.

  2. (2)

    If πk=(j)\pi_{k}=(j), then replace the first occurrence of j+1j+1 in α\alpha by jj.

The map φ\varphi is a fixed-point-free involution on UPFn∖{w0}\UPF_{n}\setminus\{w_{0}\} satisfying disp⁡(φ⁡(α))=disp⁡(α)±1\disp(\varphi(\alpha))=\disp(\alpha)\pm 1 and inv⁡(φ⁡(α))=inv⁡(α)\inv(\varphi(\alpha))=\inv(\alpha) (we omit the proof). If one associates unit interval parking functions with faces of the permutohedron, as done in [7], the function φ\varphi appears to give an acyclic matching in the sense of discrete Morse theory [14, 15].

4.2. A cyclic sieving phenomenon

Let XX be a finite set, let f⁡(t)f(t) be a polynomial in tt such that f⁡(1)=|X|f(1)=|X|, let C=⟨g⟩C=\langle g\rangle be a cyclic group of order nn acting on XX, and let ω\omega be a primitive nnth root of unity. The triple (X,f⁡(t),C)(X,f(t),C) is said to exhibit the cyclic sieving phenomenon [21] if f⁡(ωj)=|{x∈X:gj⋅x=x}|f(\omega^{j})=|\{x\in X\colon g^{j}\cdot x=x\}| for any j∈[n]j\in[n].

For a given surjective function s:[n]→[m]s:[n]\to[m] and permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n}, define

σ⋅s:=s∘σ−1.\sigma\cdot s:=s\circ\sigma^{-1}.

It is easy to check this defines an action of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} on the set of surjective functions s:[n]→[m]s:[n]\to[m]. Using the bijection in Corollary 2.11, we extend this to an action on UPFn\UPF_{n}. For example, if α=(8,1,5,5,1,2,4,7)∈UPF8\alpha=(8,1,5,5,1,2,4,7)\in\UPF_{8} and σ=(1,8)​(2,7,5)​(3,4)​(6)\sigma=(1,8)(2,7,5)(3,4)(6), then we compute σ⋅α\sigma\cdot\alpha by first turning α\alpha into the surjective function s=51331124s=51331124, computing σ⋅s=41332115\sigma\cdot s=41332115, and then converting back to (7,1,5,5,4,2,1,8).(7,1,5,5,4,2,1,8). We can further see that two UPFs are in the same orbit of this 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action if and only if they have the same block structure. This action is considered implicitly in [7] as an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action on the faces of the permutohedron.

We restrict the above 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action on UPFn\UPF_{n} to the cyclic CnC_{n} generated by the nn-cycle g:=(1,2,…,n)g:=(1,2,\dots,n). For cyclic sieving, we need to characterize the fixed points of the action.

Lemma 4.6.

Let α=(a1,…,an)∈UPFn\alpha=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\in\UPF_{n}, let jj be a divisor of nn, and suppose n=j​d.n=jd.

  1. (1)

    gj⋅α=αg^{j}\cdot\alpha=\alpha if and only if for each i∈[n]i\in[n], the entries

    ai,ai+j,…,ai+(d−1)​j,a_{i},a_{i+j},\dots,a_{i+(d-1)j},

    where the indices are taken modulo nn, all belong to the same block.

  2. (2)

    If n=j​dn=jd and α\alpha has block structure π1|π2​|⋯|​πm\pi_{1}|\pi_{2}|\cdots|\pi_{m}, then there are

    (n/d|π1|/d,|π2|/d,…,|πm|/d)\binom{n/d}{|\pi_{1}|/d,|\pi_{2}|/d,\dots,|\pi_{m}|/d}

    elements in the 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-orbit of α\alpha that are fixed by gjg^{j}, where we adopt the convention that any multinomial expression involving one or more non-integers is zero.

Proof.

Let ss be the corresponding surjective function of α\alpha. Since gj⋅α=αg^{j}\cdot\alpha=\alpha if and only if gj⋅s=sg^{j}\cdot s=s, and (gj⋅s)​(i)=s⁡(g−j​(i))=s⁡(i+j),(g^{j}\cdot s)(i)=s(g^{-j}(i))=s(i+j), we have that gj⋅α=αg^{j}\cdot\alpha=\alpha if and only if s⁡(i)=s⁡(i+j)s(i)=s(i+j) for all ii. Claim (1) then follows from translating back to UPFs.

For claim (2), if gj⋅s=sg^{j}\cdot s=s, then by part (1), the entire function is determined by its restriction s|[j].s|_{[j]}. This is also a surjective function s|[j]:[j]→[m]s|_{[j]}:[j]\to[m] and the corresponding UPF in UPFj\UPF_{j} has blocks of sizes |π1|/d,…,|πm|/d|\pi_{1}|/d,\dots,|\pi_{m}|/{d}. Recall that for a composition c=(c1,…,cℓ)c=(c_{1},\dots,c_{\ell}) of nn, the tt-multinomial coefficient is

[nc1,c2,…,cℓ]t:=[n]t![c1]t![c2]t!⋯[cℓ]t!,\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{c_1,c_2,\dots,c_\ell}_{t}:=\frac{[n]_{t}!}{[c_{1}]_{t}![c_{2}]_{t}!\cdots[c_{\ell}]_{t}!},

Theorem 4.7.

The triple (UPFn,kdisp,fn,kdisp​(t),Cn)(\UPF_{n,k}^{\disp},f_{n,k}^{\disp}(t),C_{n}) satisfies the cyclic sieving phenomenon for each nn and kk. That is, for all n,k,jn,k,j, if ω\omega is a primitive nnth root of unity, then,

Corollary 4.8.

Let nn be a positive integer.

  1. (1)

    If ω\omega is a primitive nnth root of unity, then

    Φn,1​(q,ω)=∑α∈UPFnqdisp⁡(α)​ωinv⁡(α)=qn−1.\Phi_{n,1}(q,\omega)=\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}q^{\disp(\alpha)}\omega^{\inv(\alpha)}=q^{n-1}.

    Φn,1​(q,−1)=∑α∈UPFnqdisp⁡(α)​(−1)inv⁡(α)=qn/2​∑α∈UPFn/2qdisp⁡(α).\Phi_{n,1}(q,-1)=\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}q^{\disp(\alpha)}(-1)^{\inv(\alpha)}=q^{n/2}\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n/2}}q^{\disp(\alpha)}.

(1) This is the case j=1j=1 of Theorem 4.7. A UPF is fixed by gg if and only if it has a single block of size nn. There is exactly one such UPF, namely α=(1,1,2,…,n−1)\alpha=(1,1,2,\dots,n-1), which has total displacement n−1n-1.

(2) Define UPFn2\UPF^{2}_{n} to be the set of unit interval parking functions whose block sizes are all divisible by 2 and let UPFn2↑=UPFn2∩UPFn↑\UPF_{n}^{2\uparrow}=\UPF_{n}^{2}\cap\UPF_{n}^{\uparrow}. Since an increasing UPF is determined by its list of block sizes, in order, there is a bijection ρ:UPFn2↑→UPFn/2↑\rho\colon\UPF_{n}^{2\uparrow}\to\UPF_{n/2}^{\uparrow} given by dividing all block sizes by 2. (For instance, ρ⁡(1123​∣55∣​7789)=11​∣3∣​44\rho(1123\mid 55\mid 7789)=11\mid 3\mid 44, because these are the unique increasing UPFs with block sizes 4,2,44,2,4 and 2,1,22,1,2 respectively.) Note also that disp⁡(β)=disp⁡(ρ⁡(β))+n/2\disp(\beta)=\disp(\rho(\beta))+n/2. Now substituting j=n/2j=n/2 in (19) yields

∑α∈UPFnqdisp⁡(α)​(−1)inv⁡(α)\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}q^{\disp(\alpha)}(-1)^{\inv(\alpha)} =∑β∈UPFn2↑qdisp⁡(β)​(n/2|πβ1|/2,πβ2|/2,…,|πβmβ|/2)\displaystyle=\sum_{\beta\in\UPF_{n}^{2\uparrow}}q^{\disp(\beta)}\binom{n/2}{|\pi^{\beta}_{1}|/2,\pi^{\beta}_{2}|/2,\;\dots,\;|\pi^{\beta}_{m_{\beta}}|/2}
=qn/2​∑α∈UPFn/2↑qdisp⁡(α)​(n/2|π1α|,|π2α|,…,|πmαα|)\displaystyle=q^{n/2}\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n/2}^{\uparrow}}q^{\disp(\alpha)}\binom{n/2}{|\pi^{\alpha}_{1}|,|\pi^{\alpha}_{2}|,\;\dots,\;|\pi^{\alpha}_{m_{\alpha}}|} (setting α=ϕ⁡(β)\alpha=\phi(\beta))
=qn/2​∑α∈UPFn/2qdisp⁡(α),\displaystyle=q^{n/2}\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n/2}}q^{\disp(\alpha)},

where the last step follows from (19), replacing nn and jj with n/2n/2 and dd with 1. ∎

4.3. From ℓ=1\ell=1 to ℓ=2\ell=2

Theorem 4.4 can be viewed as reducing the enumeration of 11-interval parking functions to the enumeration of 00-interval parking functions, which are just permutations. We now describe a similar reduction from 22-interval parking functions to 11-interval parking functions, although it is more complicated.

Let β=(b1,b2,…,bn)∈UPFn\beta=(b_{1},b_{2},\ldots,b_{n})\in\UPF_{n} have block structure π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πm\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{m}. Let ℛ⁡(β)\mathcal{R}(\beta) be the set of numbers i∈[n]i\in[n] such that bib_{i} is the second entry in its block πj\pi_{j}, where j>1j>1, and bib_{i} occurs after the last entry of block πj−1\pi_{j-1} Let 𝒮⁡(β)\mathcal{S}(\beta) be the set of numbers i∈[n]i\in[n] such that bib_{i} is the third or later entry in its block πj\pi_{j}. Then

(22) |𝒮⁡(β)|=∑i=1mmax⁡(|πi|−2,0).|\mathcal{S}(\beta)|=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\max(|\pi_{i}|-2,0).
Example 4.9.

If β=7511278935∈UPF10\beta=7511278935\in\UPF_{10}, then its block structure is π1​∣π2∣​π3=1123​∣55∣​7789\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\pi_{3}=1123\mid 55\mid 7789. The second entry in block π2\pi_{2} is b10=5b_{10}=5 and appears after the last entry of π1\pi_{1}, which is b9=3b_{9}=3. Hence, 10∈ℛ⁡(β)10\in\mathcal{R}(\beta). The second entry in block π3\pi_{3} is b6=7b_{6}=7 and does not appear after the last entry of π2\pi_{2}. Hence, we can see that 6∉ℛ⁡(β)6\notin\mathcal{R}(\beta). Thus, we have ℛ⁡(β)={10}\mathcal{R}(\beta)=\{10\}. Lastly, in block π1=1123\pi_{1}=1123 the third or later entries are b5=2b_{5}=2 and b9=3b_{9}=3, while in block π3=7789\pi_{3}=7789 the third or later entries are b7=8b_{7}=8 and b8=9b_{8}=9. We then get that 𝒮⁡(7511278935)={5,7,8,9}\mathcal{S}(7511278935)=\{5,7,8,9\}. We have |𝒮⁡(β)|=2+0+2=4|\mathcal{S}(\beta)|=2+0+2=4, which as expected by (22).

Observe that

(23) ℛ⁡(β)∩𝒮⁡(β)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\beta)\cap\mathcal{S}(\beta) =∅,and\displaystyle=\emptyset,\ \text{and}
(24) ℛ⁡(β)∪𝒮⁡(β)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\beta)\cup\mathcal{S}(\beta) ={i∈[2,n]: spots bi−1 and bi are both occupied when car i parks}.\displaystyle=\{i\in[2,n]\colon\text{ spots $b_{i}-1$ and $b_{i}$ are both occupied when car $i$ parks}\}.

In particular, if i∈R⁡(β)i\in R(\beta), then spot bi−1b_{i}-1 is occupied by the last car of block πj−1\pi_{j-1}, and spot bib_{i} by the first car of block πj\pi_{j}.

Example 4.10.

Continuing Example 4.9, let β=7511278935\beta=7511278935 and we can confirm ℛ⁡(β)∩𝒮⁡(β)=∅\mathcal{R}(\beta)\cap\mathcal{S}(\beta)=\emptyset. One can readily confirm that the only indices i∈[2,n]i\in[2,n] such that spots bi−1b_{i}-1 and bib_{i} are occupied when car ii parks are precisely the indices i∈{5,7,8,9,10}=ℛ⁡(β)∪𝒮⁡(β)i\in\{5,7,8,9,10\}=\mathcal{R}(\beta)\cup\mathcal{S}(\beta). For example, when car 77 parks, spots b7−1=8−1=7b_{7}-1=8-1=7 and b7=8b_{7}=8 are occupied by cars 11 and 66, respectively.

Define a map η:IPFn⁡(2)→UPFn\eta:\IPF_{n}(2)\to\UPF_{n} by

η​(α)i={ai+1dispα⁡(i)=2,aidispα⁡(i)≤1.\eta(\alpha)_{i}=\begin{cases}a_{i}+1&\disp_{\alpha}(i)=2,\\ a_{i}&\disp_{\alpha}(i)\leq 1.\\ \end{cases}

Informally, we obtain η⁡(α)\eta(\alpha) by asking each car with displacement 2, “Please lower your expectations by one spot.” It is unsurprising, though not entirely obvious, that the result is a unit interval parking function with the same spot permutation, as we now prove.

Lemma 4.11.

Let α∈IPFn⁡(2)\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(2) and β=η⁡(α)\beta=\eta(\alpha). Then β∈UPFn\beta\in\UPF_{n}, and spotβ=spotα\spot_{\beta}=\spot_{\alpha}.

Proof.

We show by induction that spotβ⁡(i)=spotα⁡(i)\spot_{\beta}(i)=\spot_{\alpha}(i) and dispβ⁡(i)≤1\disp_{\beta}(i)\leq 1 for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. For i=1i=1, we have dispα⁡(1)=0\disp_{\alpha}(1)=0, so b1=a1=spotβ⁡(1)=spotβ⁡(1)b_{1}=a_{1}=\spot_{\beta}(1)=\spot_{\beta}(1). For the inductive step, suppose that spotα⁡(j)=spotβ⁡(j)\spot_{\alpha}(j)=\spot_{\beta}(j) for all j<ij<i.

  • •

    If dispα⁡(i)≤1\disp_{\alpha}(i)\leq 1, then bi=aib_{i}=a_{i} and spotβ⁡(i)=spotα⁡(i)\spot_{\beta}(i)=\spot_{\alpha}(i); in particular, dispβ⁡(i)≤1\disp_{\beta}(i)\leq 1.

  • •

    If dispα⁡(i)=2\disp_{\alpha}(i)=2, then spotα⁡(i)=ai+2\spot_{\alpha}(i)=a_{i}+2. In particular, spots aia_{i} and ai+1a_{i}+1 are full when car ii parks. Changing the preference of the iith car from aia_{i} to bi=ai+1b_{i}=a_{i}+1 does not affect where car ii parks, but then dispβ⁡(i)=ai+2−bi=1\disp_{\beta}(i)=a_{i}+2-b_{i}=1.∎

We now prove our main enumeration result on 22-interval parking functions.

Theorem 4.12.

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

Φn,2​(q,t)=∑β∈UPFnqdisp⁡(β)​tinv⁡(β)​(1+q)|𝒮⁡(β)|​(1+q​t)|ℛ⁡(β)|.\Phi_{n,2}(q,t)=\sum_{\beta\in\UPF_{n}}q^{\disp(\beta)}t^{\inv(\beta)}(1+q)^{|\mathcal{S}(\beta)|}(1+qt)^{|\mathcal{R}(\beta)|}.

In particular,

|IPFn⁡(2)|=∑β∈UPFn2|𝒮⁡(β)|+|ℛ⁡(β)|.|\IPF_{n}(2)|=\sum_{\beta\in\UPF_{n}}2^{|\mathcal{S}(\beta)|+|\mathcal{R}(\beta)|}.
Proof.

Let β=(b1,b2,…,bn)∈UPFn\beta=(b_{1},b_{2},\ldots,b_{n})\in\UPF_{n} have block structure π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πm\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{m}. Let ℛ=ℛ⁡(β)\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}(\beta) and 𝒮=𝒮⁡(β)\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}(\beta). For R⊆ℛR\subseteq\mathcal{R} and S⊆𝒮S\subseteq\mathcal{S}, define α=(a1,a2,…,an)=gβ​(R,S)\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})=g_{\beta}(R,S) by

ai={bi−1 if ​i∈R∪S,bi if ​i∉R∪S.a_{i}=\begin{cases}b_{i}-1&\text{ if }i\in R\cup S,\\ b_{i}&\text{ if }i\not\in R\cup S.\end{cases}

Then α\alpha is a parking function by the rearrangement criterion. In light of the description of ℛ∪𝒮\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{S} in (24), it follows that for all i∈[n]i\in[n],

(25a) i∈R∪S\displaystyle i\in R\cup S if and only if ​dispα​(i)=2;\displaystyle\mbox{ if and only if }\disp_{\alpha}(i)=2;
(25b) i∉R∪S\displaystyle i\not\in R\cup S if and only if ​dispα⁡(i)≤1;\displaystyle\mbox{ if and only if }\disp_{\alpha}(i)\leq 1;
(25c) spotα⁡(i)\displaystyle\spot_{\alpha}(i) =spotβ⁡(i).\displaystyle=\spot_{\beta}(i).

It follows that α∈η−1​(β)⊆IPFn⁡(2)\alpha\in\eta^{-1}(\beta)\subseteq\IPF_{n}(2). This defines a function

gβ:2ℛ×2𝒮→η−1​(β).g_{\beta}\colon 2^{\mathcal{R}}\times 2^{\mathcal{S}}\to\eta^{-1}(\beta).

We claim that gβg_{\beta} is a bijection. It is injective since ℛ∩𝒮=∅\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{S}=\emptyset. To show that gβg_{\beta} is surjective, it suffices to show that if α∈η−1​(β)\alpha\in\eta^{-1}(\beta) and dispα⁡(i)=2\disp_{\alpha}(i)=2, then i∈ℛ∪𝒮i\in\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{S}. Indeed, we have bi=ai+1b_{i}=a_{i}+1 by definition of η\eta. Since dispα⁡(i)=2\disp_{\alpha}(i)=2, when car ii parks, spots ai=bi−1a_{i}=b_{i}-1 and ai+1=bia_{i}+1=b_{i} are both occupied, and since spotα=spotβ\spot_{\alpha}=\spot_{\beta} by Lemma 4.11, we have i∈ℛ∪𝒮i\in\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{S} by (24).

Note that the inverse map fβ=gβ−1f_{\beta}=g_{\beta}^{-1} is given by fβ​(α)=(R,S)f_{\beta}(\alpha)=(R,S), where

R=ℛ∩{i∈[n]:dispα⁡(i)=2},and ​S=𝒮∩{i∈[n]:dispα⁡(i)=2}.R=\mathcal{R}\cap\{i\in[n]\colon\disp_{\alpha}(i)=2\},~\mbox{and }S=\mathcal{S}\cap\{i\in[n]\colon\disp_{\alpha}(i)=2\}.

Now, let β∈UPFn\beta\in\UPF_{n}, and let α=gβ​(R,S)\alpha=g_{\beta}(R,S) for some R⊆ℛ⁡(β)R\subseteq\mathcal{R}(\beta) and S⊆𝒮⁡(β)S\subseteq\mathcal{S}(\beta). Then

dispα⁡(i)={dispβ⁡(i) if ​i∉R∪S,dispβ⁡(i)+1 if ​i∈R∪S,\disp_{\alpha}(i)=\begin{cases}\disp_{\beta}(i)&\text{ if }i\notin R\cup S,\\ \disp_{\beta}(i)+1&\text{ if }i\in R\cup S,\end{cases}

so

(26) disp⁡(α)=disp⁡(β)+|R|+|S|.\disp(\alpha)=\disp(\beta)+|R|+|S|.

We now describe inv⁡(α)\inv(\alpha) in terms of inv⁡(β)\inv(\beta). Suppose for contradiction that (i,j)(i,j) is an inversion of β\beta but not of α\alpha. Then, by the definition of gβg_{\beta}, we have i∈R∪Si\in R\cup S, j∉R∪Sj\not\in R\cup S, and bi=bj+1b_{i}=b_{j}+1. Hence, ai=bi−1=bj=aja_{i}=b_{i}-1=b_{j}=a_{j}. Since β\beta is a unit interval parking function, it does not have inversions within blocks (Theorem 2.10, part (2)); hence, bib_{i} and bjb_{j} must be in different blocks. Thus, bib_{i} is either the first or second element of some block πk+1\pi_{k+1} and bjb_{j} is the last element of block πk\pi_{k}. If bib_{i} is the first element of πk+1\pi_{k+1}, then i∉ℛ∪𝒮.i\notin\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{S}. If bib_{i} is the second element of πk+1\pi_{k+1} then again i∉ℛ∪𝒮i\notin\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{S} because bib_{i} occurs before the only entry of πk\pi_{k}, namely bj.b_{j}. Hence, we get that i∉ℛ∪𝒮i\notin\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{S}, which is a contradiction. We conclude that Inv⁡(β)⊆Inv⁡(α).\Inv(\beta)\subseteq\Inv(\alpha).

Now suppose that (i,j)(i,j) is an inversion of α\alpha but not of β\beta. Then we have by definition of gβg_{\beta} that i∉R∪Si\not\in R\cup S, j∈R∪Sj\in R\cup S and bi=bjb_{i}=b_{j}. Hence, j∈Rj\in R because it is the second occurrence of the same number (since i<ji<j) and thus is the second entry of its block. Conversely, whenever bi=bjb_{i}=b_{j} with i<ji<j and j∈Rj\in R, the pair (i,j)(i,j) is an inversion of α\alpha but not of β\beta. Therefore,

(27) inv⁡(α)=inv⁡(β)+|R|.\inv(\alpha)=\inv(\beta)+|R|.

and combining (26) and (27) we obtain

(28) qdisp⁡(α)​tinv⁡(α)=qdisp⁡(β)+|R|+|S|​tinv⁡(β)+|R|.q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\inv(\alpha)}=q^{\disp(\beta)+|R|+|S|}t^{\inv(\beta)+|R|}.

Consequently,

∑α∈η−1​(β)qdisp⁡(α)​tinv⁡(α)\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\eta^{-1}(\beta)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\inv(\alpha)} =∑R⊆ℛ∑S⊆𝒮qdisp⁡(β)+|R|+|S|​tinv⁡(β)+|R|\displaystyle=\sum_{R\subseteq\mathcal{R}}\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{S}}q^{\disp(\beta)+|R|+|S|}t^{\inv(\beta)+|R|}
=qdisp⁡(β)​tinv⁡(β)​(∑R⊆ℛ(q​t)|R|)​(∑S⊆𝒮q|S|)\displaystyle=q^{\disp(\beta)}t^{\inv(\beta)}\left(\sum_{R\subseteq\mathcal{R}}(qt)^{|R|}\right)\left(\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{S}}q^{|S|}\right)
=qdisp⁡(β)​tinv⁡(β)​(1+q)|𝒮⁡(β)|​(1+q​t)|ℛ⁡(β)|,\displaystyle=q^{\disp(\beta)}t^{\inv(\beta)}(1+q)^{|\mathcal{S}(\beta)|}(1+qt)^{|\mathcal{R}(\beta)|},

and summing over all β∈UPFn\beta\in\UPF_{n} yields the theorem. ∎

Example 4.13.

Let β=6411624∈UPF7\beta=6411624\in\UPF_{7}, which has block structure β↑=112​|44|​66\beta^{\uparrow}=112|44|66. Positions 4,5,7 contain the second elements of the blocks. Note that ℛ⁡(β)={7}\mathcal{R}(\beta)=\{7\}, because:

    7∈ℛ⁡(β)7\in\mathcal{R}(\beta) because the 4 in position 7 is the second element of π2\pi_{2}, and it occurs to the right of the largest element of π1\pi_{1}, namely the 2 in position 5.

spotβ=6412735,disp⁡(β)=0+0+0+1+1+1+1=4,inv⁡(β)=|{12,13,14,16,17,23,24,26,56,57}|=10.\spot_{\beta}=6412735,\quad\disp(\beta)=0+0+0+1+1+1+1=4,\quad\inv(\beta)=|\{12,13,14,16,17,23,24,26,56,57\}|=10.

RSαspotαdisp⁡(α)∅∅641162464127350+0+0+1+1+1+1=47∅6​4¯​1162​3¯64127350+0+0+1+1+1+2=5∅6641161464127350+0+0+1+1+2+1=5766​4¯​1161​3¯64127350+0+0+1+1+2+2=6\begin{array}[]{ccccc}R&S&\alpha&\spot_{\alpha}&\disp(\alpha)\\ \hline\cr\emptyset&\emptyset&6411624&6412735&0+0+0+1+1+1+1=4\\ 7&\emptyset&6\underline{4}1162\underline{3}&6412735&0+0+0+1+1+1+2=5\\ \emptyset&6&6411614&6412735&0+0+0+1+1+2+1=5\\ 7&6&6\underline{4}1161\underline{3}&6412735&0+0+0+1+1+2+2=6\end{array}

Since Φn,2​(q,t)\Phi_{n,2}(q,t) can be understood as enumerating 22-interval parking functions by either displacement and inversions or by displacement and major index, it is natural to want a version of Theorem 4.12 that involves maj⁡(β)\maj(\beta) instead of inv⁡(β)\inv(\beta). To obtain this from Theorem 4.12 and Theorem 3.1, we must study what happens to |ℛ⁡(β)||\mathcal{R}(\beta)| and |𝒮⁡(β)||\mathcal{S}(\beta)| when we apply the Foata transfrom to a unit interval parking function β\beta. It turns out that these do not change, as the following lemma will help us show.

Lemma 4.14.

Let (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. Let j,k∈[n]j,k\in[n] such that aj≤aka_{j}\leq a_{k}, and let i≥max⁡(j,k)i\geq\max(j,k).

  1. (1)

    If ai+1∉{aj,…,ak−1}a_{i+1}\not\in\{a_{j},\dots,a_{k}-1\}, then aja_{j} and aka_{k} appear in the same order in F(a1a2⋯ai+1)F(a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{i+1}) as they do in F(a1a2⋯ai)F(a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{i}).

  2. (2)

    If {aj,…,ak−1}∩{ai+1,…,an}=∅\{a_{j},\dots,a_{k}-1\}\cap\{a_{i+1},\dots,a_{n}\}=\emptyset, then aja_{j} and aka_{k} appear in the same order in F(a1⋯an)F(a_{1}\cdots a_{n}) as they do in F(a1a2⋯ai)F(a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{i}).

Proof.

(1) The condition ai+1∉{aj,…,ak−1}a_{i+1}\not\in\{a_{j},\dots,a_{k}-1\} implies that, at the (i+1)(i+1)st stage of the algorithm, separators are placed either after both aja_{j} and aka_{k}, or after neither. If both, then aja_{j} and aka_{k} belong to different segments. If neither, then if they are in the same segment, then neither one is the last entry in that segment. Therefore, in all cases, the cycling step maintains the relative position of aja_{j} and aka_{k}, so they appear in the same order in F(a1⋯ai+1)F(a_{1}\cdots a_{i+1}) as in F(a1⋯ai)F(a_{1}\cdots a_{i}).

(2) This claim follows from applying (1) repeatedly. ∎

Lemma 4.15.

If α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n}, then |ℛ⁡(α)|=|ℛ⁡(F⁡(α))||\mathcal{R}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{R}(F(\alpha))| and |𝒮⁡(α)|=|𝒮⁡(F⁡(α))|.|\mathcal{S}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{S}(F(\alpha))|.

Proof.

Since FF preserves content, it preserves block structure, and so we have |𝒮⁡(α)|=|𝒮⁡(F⁡(α))||\mathcal{S}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{S}(F(\alpha))| by (22).

For α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈UPFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\UPF_{n}, let 𝒫⁡(α)\mathcal{P}(\alpha) be the set of positions of the second entries of blocks. Equivalently, by block structure,

𝒫⁡(α)={i∈[n]:aj=ai​ for some ​j<i}.\mathcal{P}(\alpha)=\{i\in[n]\colon a_{j}=a_{i}\text{ for some }j<i\}.

Note that ℛ⁡(α)⊆𝒫⁡(α)\mathcal{R}(\alpha)\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\alpha). Moreover, we have |𝒫⁡(α)|=|𝒫⁡(F⁡(α))||\mathcal{P}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{P}(F(\alpha))| because FF preserves content. For convenience, define ℛ′​(α)={ai:i∈ℛ⁡(α)}\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(\alpha)=\{a_{i}\colon i\in\mathcal{R}(\alpha)\}, so that |ℛ′​(α)|=|ℛ⁡(α)||\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{R}(\alpha)|.

We claim that ℛ′​(α)=ℛ′​(F⁡(α))\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(\alpha)=\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(F(\alpha)). Indeed, let k∈𝒫⁡(α)k\in\mathcal{P}(\alpha), and let πs\pi_{s} be the block containing aka_{k}. Taking aja_{j} to be either the first entry of πs\pi_{s} or the last entry of πs−1\pi_{s-1}, and taking i=max⁡(j,k)i=\max(j,k), block structure implies that the elements aj,aka_{j},a_{k} satisfy the conditions of Lemma 4.14, hence appear in the same order in F⁡(α)F(\alpha) as they do in F(a1a2⋯ai)F(a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{i}), hence the same order as in a1⋯aia_{1}\cdots a_{i} (due to our choice of ii). In particular, ak∈ℛ′​(α)a_{k}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(\alpha) if and only if ak∈ℛ′​(F⁡(α))a_{k}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(F(\alpha)). Therefore,

|ℛ⁡(α)|=|ℛ′​(α)|=|ℛ′​(F⁡(α))|=|ℛ⁡(F⁡(α))|.∎|\mathcal{R}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(F(\alpha))|=|\mathcal{R}(F(\alpha))|.\qed
