Let α=34411∈UPF5\alpha=34411\in\UPF_{5}, with block structure 11​∣3∣​4411\mid 3\mid 44. Then F⁡(α)=13441F(\alpha)=13441. Note that

𝒫⁡(α)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\alpha) ={3,5},\displaystyle=\{3,5\}, ℛ⁡(α)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\alpha) ={3},\displaystyle=\{3\},
𝒫⁡(F⁡(α))\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(F(\alpha)) ={4,5},\displaystyle=\{4,5\}, ℛ⁡(F⁡(α))\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(F(\alpha)) ={4},\displaystyle=\{4\},

and ℛ′​(α)=ℛ′​(F⁡(α))={4}\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(\alpha)=\mathcal{R}^{\prime}(F(\alpha))=\{4\}.

Applying Lemma 4.15 and Theorem 3.1 to Theorem 4.12, we obtain a major-index enumeration for 22-interval parking functions.

Corollary 4.17.

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

∑α∈IPFn⁡(2)qdisp⁡(α)​tmaj⁡(α)=∑β∈UPFnqdisp⁡(β)​(1+q)|𝒮⁡(β)|​(1+q​t)|ℛ⁡(β)|​tmaj⁡(β).\sum_{\alpha\in\IPF_{n}(2)}q^{\disp(\alpha)}t^{\maj(\alpha)}=\sum_{\beta\in\UPF_{n}}q^{\disp(\beta)}(1+q)^{|\mathcal{S}(\beta)|}(1+qt)^{|\mathcal{R}(\beta)|}t^{\maj(\beta)}.

5. Enumeration via ciphers

For positive integer nn and nonnegative integer kk, define

UPFn,kinv={α∈UPFn:inv⁡(α)=k},upfn,kinv=|UPFn,kinv|.\UPF_{n,k}^{\inv}=\{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}\colon\inv(\alpha)=k\},\quad\upf_{n,k}^{\inv}=|\UPF_{n,k}^{\inv}|.

Setting q=1q=1 in Theorem 4.4 and extracting the coefficient of tkt^{k} yields

(29) upfn,kinv=∑σ∈𝔖ninv⁡(σ)=k2asc⁡(σ)\upf_{n,k}^{\inv}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\ \inv(\sigma)=k\end{subarray}}2^{\asc(\sigma)}

although it is not clear how to convert this expression to a closed formula. In this section, we describe how work of Avalos and Bly [4], together with block structure theory (Theorem 2.10), can be used to determine the numbers upfn,kinv\upf_{n,k}^{\inv} through the use of ciphers, an analogue of Lehmer codes for unit interval parking functions. We then use ciphers to provide a new proof of [10, Theorem 1.2], which counts Boolean intervals of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} under the right weak order by certain unit interval parking functions.

5.1. The Avalos–Bly and cipher bijections

Let mm and nn be nonnegative integers. In what follows, T=(T1,T2,…,Tm)T=(T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{m}) always denotes an ordered list of multisets of nonnegative integers. Let type⁡(T)=(|T1|,|T2|,…,|Tm|)\type(T)=(|T_{1}|,|T_{2}|,\dots,|T_{m}|). Following Avalos and Bly [4, Defns. 1.8, 1.10], define

ℱnm\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n} ={T=(T1,T2,…,Tm):|T1|+|T2|+⋯+|Tm|=n​ and ​0≤x≤∑j=1i−1|Tj|​ for all ​x∈Ti},\displaystyle=\{T=(T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{m})\colon|T_{1}|+|T_{2}|+\cdots+|T_{m}|=n\text{ and }0\leq x\leq\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}|T_{j}|\text{ for all }x\in T_{i}\},
ℱnm​(k)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}(k) ={T=(T1,T2,…,Tm)∈ℱnm:∑i∑x∈Tix=k}.\displaystyle=\{T=(T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{m})\in\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}\colon\sum_{i}\sum_{x\in T_{i}}x=k\}.

Avalos and Bly proved [4, Proposition 1.9] that there is a bijection

φ:[m]n→ℱnm\varphi\colon[m]^{n}\to\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}

defined as follows. Given w=(w1,w2,…,wn)∈[m]nw=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in[m]^{n} and j∈[n]j\in[n], define

(30) inv⁡(w,j)=|{ℓ∈[j+1,n]:wj>wℓ}|\inv(w,j)=|\{\ell\in[j+1,n]\colon w_{j}>w_{\ell}\}|

(the number of inversions with wjw_{j} as the left element). Let Ti={inv⁡(w,j):wj=i}T_{i}=\{\inv(w,j)\colon w_{j}=i\} (as a multiset) and set φ⁡(w)=(T1,T2,…,Tm)\varphi(w)=(T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{m}). In particular, since inv⁡(w)=∑j=1minv⁡(w,j)\inv(w)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\inv(w,j), it follows that φ\varphi restricts to a bijection

{w∈[m]n:inv⁡(w)=k}→ℱnm​(k),\{w\in[m]^{n}\colon\inv(w)=k\}\to\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}(k),

which is [4, Proposition 1.11]. Define the content of w∈[m]nw\in[m]^{n} as cont⁡(w)=(|w−1​(1)|,…,|w−1​(m)|)\cont(w)=(|w^{-1}(1)|,\dots,|w^{-1}(m)|) (regarding ww as a map w:[n]→[m]w:[n]\to[m]). Then the Avalos–Bly construction implies that type⁡(T)=cont⁡(w)\type(T)=\cont(w). In particular, for each weak integer composition cc of nn, the map φ\varphi restricts to bijections

(31) {w∈[m]n:cont⁡(w)=c}\displaystyle\{w\in[m]^{n}\colon\cont(w)=c\} →{T∈ℱnm:type⁡(T)=c},\displaystyle\to\{T\in\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}\colon\type(T)=c\},
{w∈[m]n:cont(w)=c,inv(w)=k}\displaystyle\{w\in[m]^{n}\colon\cont(w)=c,\ \inv(w)=k\} →{T∈ℱnm​(k):type⁡(T)=c}.\displaystyle\to\{T\in\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}(k)\colon\type(T)=c\}.

Combining the Avalos–Bly bijections (31) with that of Corollary 2.11, we obtain bijections

{α∈UPFn:(|π1|,…,|πm|)=c}\displaystyle\{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}\colon(|\pi_{1}|,\dots,|\pi_{m}|)=c\} →{T∈ℱnm:type⁡(T)=c},\displaystyle\to\{T\in\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}\colon\type(T)=c\},
{α∈UPFn,kinv:(|π1|,…,|πm|)=c}\displaystyle\{\alpha\in\UPF_{n,k}^{\inv}\colon(|\pi_{1}|,\dots,|\pi_{m}|)=c\} →{T∈ℱnm​(k):type⁡(T)=c},\displaystyle\to\{T\in\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}(k)\colon\type(T)=c\},

for each (strict) integer composition cc. We can now state the main result of this section, which follows from gluing these last bijections together over all integer compositions cc.

Theorem 5.1 (Cipher Bijection).

Let nn and mm be positive integers and let kk be a nonnegative integer. Then

(32) ψ:UPFn,kinv→⋃m=1n𝒢nm​(k),\psi\colon\UPF_{n,k}^{\inv}\to\bigcup_{m=1}^{n}\mathcal{G}^{m}_{n}(k),

where

𝒢nm​(k)={(T1,T2,…,Tm)∈ℱnm​(k):|Ti|>0​ for all ​i}\mathcal{G}^{m}_{n}(k)=\{(T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{m})\in\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}(k)\colon|T_{i}|>0\mbox{ for all }i\}

is a bijection.

We call ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) the cipher of α\alpha. We represent ciphers by writing each TiT_{i} as a string of boldface numbers in weakly decreasing order, separated by bars. For instance, 𝟎𝟎|𝟏𝟏𝟎​|𝟑𝟏|​𝟏\boldsymbol{00\big|110\big|31\big|1} is an element of 𝒢84​(7)\mathcal{G}_{8}^{4}(7).

Example 5.2 (One inversion).

Let n≥2n\geq 2. We calculate upfn,1inv\upf_{n,1}^{\inv}. By (32), we have a bijection

UPFn,1inv→⋃m=1n𝒢nm​(1).\UPF_{n,1}^{\inv}\to\bigcup_{m=1}^{n}\mathcal{G}^{m}_{n}(1).

The right-hand side consists of sequences (T1,T2,…,Tm)(T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{m}) where each TiT_{i} is a nonempty multiset of 0’s and 1’s, containing a total of n−1n-1 0’s and one 11, with the 1 not appearing in T1T_{1} (so in particular m≥2m\geq 2). The ciphers for such a sequence are precisely those words that start with 𝟎\boldsymbol{0}, followed by some permutation of the following substrings: one copy of |𝟏\boldsymbol{\big|1}, and n−2n-2 more strings each of which can be either 𝟎\boldsymbol{0} or |𝟎\boldsymbol{\big|0}. The number of such ciphers is thus

(33) upfn,1inv=2n−2​(n−1).\upf_{n,1}^{\inv}=2^{n-2}(n-1).
Example 5.3 (Two inversions).

Let n≥3n\geq 3. We calculate upfn,2inv\upf_{n,2}^{\inv}. Here are the possibilities:

  1. (1)

    The cipher has one 𝟐\boldsymbol{2} and n−1n-1 𝟎\boldsymbol{0}’s. Since the 22 cannot appear before the second 00, there are 2n−2​(n−2)2^{n-2}(n-2) such words.

  2. (2)

    The cipher has two 𝟏\boldsymbol{1}’s and n−2n-2 𝟎\boldsymbol{0}’s. There are two subcases:

    1. (a)

      The 𝟏\boldsymbol{1}’s are in different blocks.

    2. Count: 2n−3​(n−12)2^{n-3}\binom{n-1}{2}

    3. (b)

      The 𝟏\boldsymbol{1}’s are in the same block.

    4. Count: 2n−3​(n−2)2^{n-3}(n-2)

Adding these counts, we obtain

(34) upfn,2inv=2n−3​(3​(n−2)+(n−12))=2n−4​(n−2)​(n+5).\upf_{n,2}^{\inv}=2^{n-3}\left(3(n-2)+\binom{n-1}{2}\right)=2^{n-4}(n-2)(n+5).
Example 5.4 (Three inversions).

Let n≥3n\geq 3. We calculate upfn,3inv\upf_{n,3}^{\inv}. The descriptions of cases and their associated counts are as follows:

There is one 𝟑22⋅2n−4⋅(n−3)There is one 𝟐 and one 𝟏 and they are in the same block2⋅2n−4⋅(n−3)There is a 𝟏 in the second block and a 𝟐 in a different block2n−3⋅(n−2)There is a 𝟏 not in the second block and a 𝟐 in a different block2⋅2n−4⋅(n−3)​(n−2)There are three 𝟏’s, all in different blocks2n−4⋅(n−13)There are three 𝟏’s, and two of them are in a block together2n−4⋅(n−3)​(n−2)There are three 𝟏’s, and they are all in the same block2n−4⋅(n−3)\begin{array}[]{ll}\text{There is one $\boldsymbol{3}$}&2^{2}\cdot 2^{n-4}\cdot(n-3)\\[4.0pt] \text{There is one $\boldsymbol{2}$ and one $\boldsymbol{1}$ and they are in the same block}&2\cdot 2^{n-4}\cdot(n-3)\\[4.0pt] \text{There is a $\boldsymbol{1}$ in the second block and a $\boldsymbol{2}$ in a different block}&2^{n-3}\cdot(n-2)\\[4.0pt] \text{There is a $\boldsymbol{1}$ not in the second block and a $\boldsymbol{2}$ in a different block}&2\cdot 2^{n-4}\cdot(n-3)(n-2)\\[4.0pt] \text{There are three $\boldsymbol{1}$'s, all in different blocks}&2^{n-4}\cdot\binom{n-1}{3}\\[4.0pt] \text{There are three $\boldsymbol{1}$'s, and two of them are in a block together}&2^{n-4}\cdot(n-3)(n-2)\\[4.0pt] \text{There are three $\boldsymbol{1}$'s, and they are all in the same block}&2^{n-4}\cdot(n-3)\\[4.0pt] \end{array}

Adding up the counts, we obtain

(35) upfn,3inv=2n−4​(16​n3+2​n2−256​n−8).\upf_{n,3}^{\inv}=2^{n-4}\left(\frac{1}{6}n^{3}+2n^{2}-\frac{25}{6}n-8\right).

Comparing the formulas (33), (34), and (35), we are led to the following general conjecture, which we leave as an open problem.

Conjecture 5.5.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and k∈{0,1,…,n⁡(n−1)/2}k\in\{0,1,\dots,n(n-1)/2\}. Then upfn,kinv=O⁡(2n−2​k​nk)\upf_{n,k}^{\inv}=O(2^{n-2k}n^{k}).

5.2. Ciphers and Lehmer codes

We describe another way to construct ciphers by way of Lehmer codes for permutations. Let En,kE_{n,k} be the set of words w∈{0,1,…,n−1}nw\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}^{n} satisfying

  1. (1)

    wi≤i−1w_{i}\leq i-1 for all i∈[n]i\in[n], and

  2. (2)

    ∑i=1nwi=k\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}=k.

Then a cipher T∈𝒢n​(k)T\in\mathcal{G}_{n}(k) can be constructed from a word w∈En,kw\in E_{n,k} by inserting bars. If wi<wi+1w_{i}<w_{i+1}, we must insert a bar between wiw_{i} and wi+1w_{i+1}; otherwise, we may insert a bar. Hence, we can construct 2n−1−asc⁡(w)2^{n-1-\asc(w)} ciphers from ww, and every cipher arises in this way. It follows that

(36) upfn,kinv=∑w∈En,k2n−1−asc⁡(w).\upf_{n,k}^{\inv}=\sum_{w\in E_{n,k}}2^{n-1-\asc(w)}.

Define

En=⋃k≥0En,k={0}×{0,1}×⋯×{0,1,…,n−1}.E_{n}=\bigcup_{k\geq 0}E_{n,k}=\{0\}\times\{0,1\}\times\cdots\times\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}.

Then EnE_{n} is the set of Lehmer codes (backwards); see [23, p. 34]. There is a bijection γ:Sn→En\gamma:S_{n}\to E_{n} from permutations to Lehmer codes: given σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n}, set γ​(σ)σ⁡(i)=#⁡{ℓ∈[i−1]:(i,ℓ)∈Inv⁡(σ)}\gamma(\sigma)_{\sigma(i)}=\#\{\ell\in[i-1]:(i,\ell)\in\Inv(\sigma)\} It is not hard to see that for all σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n},

(37) Des⁡(σ−1)\displaystyle\Des(\sigma^{-1}) =Asc⁡(γ⁡(σ))\displaystyle=\Asc(\gamma(\sigma))
and
(38) ∑i=1nγ​(σ)i\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma(\sigma)_{i} =inv⁡(σ).\displaystyle=\inv(\sigma).

Applying (37) to (36) and observing that asc⁡(σ)+des⁡(σ)=n−1\asc(\sigma)+\des(\sigma)=n-1 for all σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we obtain

upfn,kinv=∑σ∈𝔖ninv⁡(σ)=k2n−des⁡(σ−1)−1=∑σ∈𝔖ninv⁡(σ)=k2asc⁡(σ),\upf_{n,k}^{\inv}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\ \inv(\sigma)=k\end{subarray}}2^{n-\des(\sigma^{-1})-1}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\ \inv(\sigma)=k\end{subarray}}2^{\asc(\sigma)},

which recovers the q=1q=1 specialization of Theorem 4.4.

Define the underlying code of a cipher T∈𝒢n​(k)T\in\mathcal{G}_{n}(k) to be the word code⁡(T)∈En\code(T)\in E_{n} obtained from TT by removing all bars. Likewise, the underlying code of a UPF α\alpha is code⁡(α)=code⁡(ψ⁡(α))\code(\alpha)=\code(\psi(\alpha)), where ψ\psi is the Avalos–Bly bijection.

Proposition 5.6.

For a unit interval parking function α\alpha, the Lehmer code of spotα\spot_{\alpha} is the underlying code of α\alpha. In particular, if β\beta is a unit interval parking function, then α\alpha and β\beta have the same spot permutation if and only if ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) and ψ⁡(β)\psi(\beta) have the same underlying code.

Proof.

Let π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πm\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{m} be the block structure of α=(a1,a2,…,an)\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}). Following Corollary 2.11, we get a surjective function s:[n]→[m]s:[n]\to[m] from α\alpha by letting s⁡(i)s(i) be the index of the block to which aia_{i} belongs.

As in the Avalos–Bly construction described above, for each i∈[m]i\in[m], let TiT_{i} denote the multiset of all numbers inv⁡(s,j)\inv(s,j) (see (30)) such that s⁡(j)=is(j)=i. Note that ψ⁡(α)=(T1,…,Tm)\psi(\alpha)=(T_{1},\dots,T_{m}) and so w:=code⁡(ψ⁡(α))w:=\code(\psi(\alpha)) is the concatenation T1T2⋯TmT_{1}T_{2}\cdots T_{m}, where each TiT_{i} is sorted in weakly decreasing order.

Let tk=|T1|+⋯+|Tk−1|t_{k}=|T_{1}|+\cdots+|T_{k-1}| and set jrj_{r} to be the index of the rrth element of ss equal to kk. For 1≤r≤|πk|1\leq r\leq|\pi_{k}|, define Tkr=inv⁡(s,jr)=|{ℓ:(jr,ℓ)∈Inv⁡(s)}|T_{k}^{r}=\inv(s,j_{r})=|\{\ell:(j_{r},\ell)\in\Inv(s)\}| so that TkT_{k} is the concatenation Tk1Tk2⋯Tk|πk|T_{k}^{1}T_{k}^{2}\cdots T_{k}^{|\pi_{k}|}. Note that {ℓ:(jr1,ℓ)∈Inv⁡(s)}⊇{ℓ:(jr2,ℓ)∈Inv⁡(s)}\{\ell:(j_{r_{1}},\ell)\in\Inv(s)\}\supseteq\{\ell:(j_{r_{2}},\ell)\in\Inv(s)\} for r1≤r2r_{1}\leq r_{2}, so that concatenation is in weakly decreasing order. In particular wtk+r=Tkrw_{t_{k}+r}=T_{k}^{r}

Since α\alpha has the same inversions as both ss and spotα\spot_{\alpha}, we have Tkr=|{ℓ:(jr,ℓ)∈Inv⁡(spotα)}|T_{k}^{r}=|\{\ell:(j_{r},\ell)\in\Inv(\spot_{\alpha})\}|. Since αjr\alpha_{j_{r}} is the rrth element of the kkst block, it will park in spot tk+rt_{k}+r. In particular, spotα⁡(jr)=tk+r\spot_{\alpha}(j_{r})=t_{k}+r. Thus,γ​(spotα)tk+r=|{ℓ:(jr,ℓ)∈Inv⁡(spotα)}|=wtk+r\gamma(\spot_{\alpha})_{t_{k}+r}=|\{\ell:(j_{r},\ell)\in\Inv(\spot_{\alpha})\}|=w_{t_{k}+r}. That is, the underlying code of α\alpha is the Lehmer code of spotα\spot_{\alpha}.

∎

Let w=00110311∈E8,7w=00110311\in E_{8,7}. 5.3. Unit Fubini rankings

A unit Fubini ranking is a unit interval parking function whose blocks all have size 1 or 2. Unit Fubini rankings were introduced in [10] to study Boolean intervals of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} under the right weak order. We can use ciphers to provide a new proof of the main result of that paper.

Theorem 5.8 ([10, Theorem 1.2]).

Unit Fubini rankings with n−rn-r blocks and kk inversions are in bijection with rank-rr Boolean intervals [σ,τ][\sigma,\tau] of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} under the right weak order with inv⁡(σ)=k\inv(\sigma)=k.

This statement is ostensibly a refinement of [10, Theorem 1.2], which does not mention inversions explicitly, but it is not difficult to use the methods of [10] together with elementary facts such as Lemma 2.14 to obtain the more refined version.

Proof.

Call a set of integers sparse if it contains no two consecutive integers. Let UFRn,km\UFR_{n,k}^{m} be the set of unit Fubini rankings of length nn with mm blocks and kk inversions. The bijection (32) restricts to a bijection

ψ:UFRn,km→ℱ^nm(k)≔{(T1,T2,…,Tm)∈ℱnm(k):|Ti|∈{1,2}for all i}.\psi\colon\UFR_{n,k}^{m}\to\hat{\mathcal{F}}^{m}_{n}(k)\coloneqq\{(T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{m})\in\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}(k)\colon|T_{i}|\in\{1,2\}\ \ \mbox{for all }i\}.

As in Example 5.7, the elements of ℱnm​(k)\mathcal{F}^{m}_{n}(k) can be represented as ciphers as follows: choose a word w∈En,kw\in E_{n,k}, insert bars at all its ascents, and insert additional bars as needed so as to obtain mm blocks, all of size 1 or 2. That means that we need a total of m−1m-1 bars; if BB is the set of non-ascents where there are bars, then |B|=m−1−|Asc⁡(w)||B|=m-1-|\Asc(w)|. Thus,we have a bijection

ℱ^nm​(k)→{(w,B):w∈En,k,B⊆[n−1]∖Asc⁡(w),|B|=m−1−|Asc⁡(w)|, and[n−1]∖(Asc⁡(w)∪B)​ is sparse}.\hat{\mathcal{F}}^{m}_{n}(k)\to\left\{(w,B)\colon\begin{array}[]{l}w\in E_{n,k},\\ B\subseteq[n-1]\setminus\Asc(w),\\ |B|=m-1-|\Asc(w)|,\mbox{ and}\\ {[n-1]}\setminus(\Asc(w)\cup B)\text{ is sparse}\end{array}\right\}.

We may replace (w,B)(w,B) with the equivalent data (σ,C)(\sigma,C), where σ=γ⁡(w)\sigma=\gamma(w) and C=Asc⁡(σ)∖BC=\Asc(\sigma)\setminus B. (By (37), we have [n−1]∖Asc⁡(w)=[n−1]∖Des⁡(σ)=Asc⁡(σ)[n-1]\setminus\Asc(w)=[n-1]\setminus\Des(\sigma)=\Asc(\sigma).) Translating the conditions on (w,B)(w,B) into conditions on (σ,C)(\sigma,C), we obtain a bijection

ℱ^nm​(k)→{(σ,C):σ∈𝔖n,inv(σ)=k,C⊆Asc(σ),|C|=n−m, and C​ is sparse}.\hat{\mathcal{F}}^{m}_{n}(k)\to\left\{(\sigma,C)\colon\begin{array}[]{l}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},\ \inv(\sigma)=k,\\ C\subseteq\Asc(\sigma),\ |C|=n-m,\mbox{ and }\\ C\text{ is sparse}\end{array}\right\}.

On the other hand, a Boolean interval in the right weak order with bottom element σ\sigma and rank rr is given precisely by choosing rr pairwise commuting elementary transpositions sis_{i} such that inv⁡(σ​si)>inv⁡(σ)\inv(\sigma s_{i})>\inv(\sigma) for every ii, which is equivalent to choosing a sparse subset of Asc⁡(σ)\Asc(\sigma) of size rr. ∎

Remark 5.9.

Let Fibi\Fib_{i} denote the iith Fibonacci number: (Fib0,Fib1,Fib2,Fib3,…)=(1,1,2,3,…)(\Fib_{0},\Fib_{1},\Fib_{2},\Fib_{3},\dots)=(1,1,2,3,\dots). Theorem 1.1 of [10] states that for each σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, the number of Boolean intervals in right weak order with bottom element σ\sigma is ∏i=1kFibai​(σ)\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Fib_{a_{i}(\sigma)}, where a1​(σ),…,ak​(σ)a_{1}(\sigma),\dots,a_{k}(\sigma) are the lengths of the maximal ascending subwords of σ=(σ1,…,σn)\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{n}), or, equivalently, of the maximal non-ascending subwords of w=γ−1​(σ−1)w=\gamma^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}). The proof of Theorem 5.8 provides a generating function for Boolean intervals by rank, as follows. Define the Fibonacci polynomials Fibn⁡(q)\Fib_{n}(q) by

Fibn⁡(q)=∑S⊆[n−1]S sparseq|S|\Fib_{n}(q)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n-1]\\ \text{$S$ sparse}\end{subarray}}q^{|S|}

(see sequence #A011973 in [18]), so that Fibn⁡(1)=Fibn\Fib_{n}(1)=\Fib_{n}. Then

(39) ∑τ∈𝔖n[σ,τ]​Booleanqinv⁡(τ)−inv⁡(σ)=∏i=1kFibai​(σ)⁡(q).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\ \ [\sigma,\tau]\ \text{Boolean}\end{subarray}}q^{\inv(\tau)-\inv(\sigma)}=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Fib_{a_{i}(\sigma)}(q).

6. Further Problems

We provide some open problems for further study.

Problem 6.1.

Describe a block structure for ℓ\ell-interval parking functions that generalizes the ℓ=1\ell=1 case (Theorem 2.10).

As we noted in Section 2.2, the block structure of unit interval parking functions appears to be unique to the case ℓ=1\ell=1. For ℓ>1\ell>1, the problem seems to be much harder.

Problem 6.2.

What can be said about the effect of the Foata transform on the outcome of a parking function?

One obvious thing is that if α∈𝔖n\alpha\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, then spotF⁡(α)=F⁡(spotα)\spot_{F(\alpha)}=F(\spot_{\alpha}) (because α=spotα\alpha=\spot_{\alpha}). However, this does not hold in general. For instance, let α=121\alpha=121. Then F⁡(α)=211F(\alpha)=211, but spotF⁡(α)=213\spot_{F(\alpha)}=213 whereas F⁡(spotα)=F⁡(123)=123.F(\spot_{\alpha})=F(123)=123. For unit interval parking functions (which the previous α\alpha is not), it seems that FF acts on the spots permutations as it did for permutations:

Conjecture 6.3.

For any unit interval parking function α\alpha, we have spotF⁡(α)=F⁡(spotα)\spot_{F(\alpha)}=F(\spot_{\alpha}).

We have verified Conjecture 6.3 for all unit interval parking functions of length at most 88.

Problem 6.4.

Count ℓ\ell-interval parking functions in terms of (ℓ±1)(\ell\pm 1)-interval parking functions.

Theorems 4.4 and 4.12 as well as Corollary 4.2 are solutions to the above problem for ℓ=1,2,n−2\ell=1,2,n-2, respectively. Let IPFn⁡(ℓ)max\IPF_{n}(\ell)^{\max} be the set of parking functions α\alpha of length nn such that maxdisp⁡(α)=ℓ\maxdisp(\alpha)=\ell. It follows from our enumerative results that for all n≥1n\geq 1

n!=|IPFn⁡(0)max|≤|IPFn⁡(1)max|≤|IPFn⁡(2)max|and|IPFn⁡(n−2)max|≥|IPFn⁡(n−1)max|=nn−2n!=|\IPF_{n}(0)^{\max}|\leq|\IPF_{n}(1)^{\max}|\leq|\IPF_{n}(2)^{\max}|\quad\text{and}\quad|\IPF_{n}(n-2)^{\max}|\geq|\IPF_{n}(n-1)^{\max}|=n^{n-2}

Experimentally, it seems this pattern continues. See Table 1.

Conjecture 6.5.

For each n≥1n\geq 1, the sequence (|IPFn⁡(ℓ)max|)ℓ=0n−1(|\IPF_{n}(\ell)^{\max}|)_{\ell=0}^{n-1} is unimodal i.e. if aℓ=|IPFn⁡(ℓ)max|a_{\ell}=|\IPF_{n}(\ell)^{\max}|, there exists an integer c∈{0,1,…,n−1}c\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\} such that

n!=a0≤a1≤a2≤⋯≤ac≥⋯≥an−2≥an−1=nn−2.n!=a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq a_{2}\leq\cdots\leq a_{c}\geq\cdots\geq a_{n-2}\geq a_{n-1}=n^{n-2}.
